marathon-490bc.title: Marathon: The Hammer of Athens
marathon-490bc.intro: In 490 BC, a Persian invasion force under Darius landed at Marathon, 25 miles from Athens. 10,000 Athenian hoplites under Miltiades faced 25,000 Persians with elite cavalry and archers. Athens charged. The world changed.
marathon-490bc.battlefieldDesc: Plain of Marathon, coast to the east, hills and marsh to the west, ~3km wide.

phases.title: The Deployment
phases.narration: The Athenians, outnumbered nearly three to one, deploy across the full width of the plain to prevent encirclement. Miltiades deliberately thins his center and stacks the wings deep, eight ranks on each flank, only four in the middle.

phases.title: The Charge
phases.narration: At a run, unprecedented for heavy infantry, Athenians cross the last 200 meters of arrow range. Speed reduces casualties from the Persian arrow storm. They strike the Persian line as one.

phases.title: The Center Yields
phases.narration: Persian elite troops, concentrated in the center, push back the thin Athenian middle. The line bends, but does not break. On the flanks, deep Athenian hoplites grind down the lighter Persian wings.

phases.title: The Wings Turn
phases.narration: Both Persian wings collapse. Instead of pursuing, the Athenian wings wheel inward and crash into the flanks and rear of the Persian center, which is still pushing forward, oblivious.

phases.title: Rout to the Ships
phases.narration: The Persian center breaks for the beaches. Athenians pursue across the marsh, where many drown in heavy armor. Seven Persian ships are captured. 6,400 Persians dead. 192 Athenians.

annotations.text: Pheidippides runs 26 miles to Athens with news of victory.

cannae-216bc.title: Cannae: Annihilation
cannae-216bc.intro: August 216 BC. Two years into Hannibal Barca's invasion of Italy, Rome musters the largest army in its history. The two consuls bring eight legions plus their Italian allies, about 86,000 men, to destroy him on the plain of Apulia. Hannibal has 50,000 men of mixed Spanish, Gallic, African, and Numidian troops. By evening, on the same dusty plain, between 50,000 and 70,000 Roman soldiers are dead. Cannae becomes the model every general since has tried to imitate.
cannae-216bc.battlefieldDesc: Apulia, southern Italy, near the village of Cannae on the south bank of the Aufidus River (modern Ofanto). A flat plain of dust. The river runs roughly east to the Adriatic. The Carthaginians face south. The Romans face north.

phases.title: The Field at Cannae
phases.narration: Consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Consul Gaius Terentius Varro share command of the largest army Rome has ever put in the field, eight legions plus their Italian allies, about 86,000 men. Hannibal Barca has roughly 50,000 of Spanish, Gauls, Africans, and Numidians. By Roman custom the consuls alternate command day by day. It is Varro's day. He drew his army in a deeper-than-usual formation, intending to overwhelm the Carthaginian center.

phases.title: Hannibal's Crescent
phases.narration: Hannibal advances his Iberian and Gallic infantry well forward of his African veterans, forming a curved bow with its convex side toward the Romans. The Africans stay back on each flank. As the Roman heavy infantry presses, the Carthaginian center will give ground in a controlled retreat. The crescent will flatten and then reverse. The Africans will become the jaws.

phases.title: Cavalry on the River
phases.narration: On the Roman right by the river, Hasdrubal's heavy cavalry drives against Paullus's smaller Roman cavalry force at close quarters in the narrow strip of ground between the infantry line and the Aufidus. Polybius writes that the fighting is on foot and 'truly barbaric.' The Roman horsemen are killed almost to a man. Paullus is wounded.

phases.title: Numidians Hold the Italian Cavalry
phases.timeMarker: during the cavalry fight on the river
phases.narration: On the opposite flank Hanno's Numidian light cavalry skirmish with the Italian allied cavalry. The Numidians do not seek to close. Their job is to fix and delay until Hasdrubal's heavy cavalry, having destroyed the Romans on the river, can wheel right across the back of the battle and join them.

phases.title: The Center Bends Back
phases.narration: The Roman heavy infantry pushes into the Carthaginian center as planned. The Iberian and Gallic line gives ground in a fighting retreat. The curved formation flattens. Then it inverts: the Carthaginian center is now bowed away from the Romans, the African heavy infantry on either flank still in their original positions. The Romans have driven themselves into a cul-de-sac without realizing it.

phases.title: The Jaws Close
phases.narration: On Hannibal's signal the African heavy infantry on each wing wheels inward, ninety degrees, and strikes the Roman flanks. The Roman packed mass cannot deploy. The men in the middle of the formation cannot use their weapons. Three sides of the Roman square are now in close combat with troops who have not yet been pressed.

phases.title: Hasdrubal Closes the Rear
phases.narration: Hasdrubal, having destroyed the Roman cavalry on the river, rides his heavy cavalry across the back of the entire battle line and falls on the rear of the Italian allied cavalry from behind. They break and flee. The Numidians pursue. Hasdrubal then turns again and charges the rear of the Roman infantry formation. The encirclement is complete.

phases.title: Annihilation
phases.narration: About 50,000 to 70,000 Roman and Italian soldiers are killed at Cannae, perhaps the deadliest single-day battle in history before the 20th century. Consul Aemilius Paullus dies on the field. So do two former consuls, the magistri equitum, eighty senators, and a dozen military tribunes. Varro escapes with a handful of survivors. The Senate refuses to ransom prisoners. Hannibal's victory is perfect. The strategic outcome, in the end, is not: Rome raises new legions, refuses to surrender, and grinds the war out for fourteen more years. Carthage will lose.

gaugamela-331bc.title: Gaugamela: Alexander's Wedge
gaugamela-331bc.intro: October 1, 331 BC. Darius III, having chosen the field and leveled the ground for his scythed chariots, fields perhaps 100,000 men. Alexander has 47,000. A single decision, a cavalry charge straight at the Persian king, decides an empire.
gaugamela-331bc.battlefieldDesc: Plain near Gaugamela in modern Iraq. Flat, scraped clear for Persian chariots.

phases.title: The Persian Host
phases.narration: Darius arrays his army on a vast prepared field: heavy cavalry on both wings, scythed chariots in front, the Royal Guard around the king at center. Persian numbers extend well beyond the Macedonian flanks.

phases.title: The Oblique March
phases.narration: Alexander marches his army diagonally to the right, dragging the Persian left out of position. He keeps his right wing refused, flanking guards angled back, so any Persian envelopment delays itself fighting.

phases.title: The Chariot Charge
phases.narration: Persian scythed chariots roar forward at the phalanx. Macedonian javelinmen and archers pick off the drivers. Disciplined infantry parts to let the horses through, then closes back up. The chariots achieve almost nothing.

phases.title: The Gap
phases.narration: Persian cavalry, pulled east chasing Alexander's drift, opens a gap in the line. Alexander wedges the Companion cavalry into the gap and aims straight at Darius, head-on, with a hammer.

phases.title: Darius Flees
phases.narration: Alexander reaches Darius. The Great King turns his chariot and flees. As word spreads through the Persian center, the army disintegrates from the head down. The empire is decapitated in a single moment.

phases.title: Parmenion Held
phases.narration: On the Macedonian left, Parmenion held against a desperate Persian right wing until Alexander could disengage from the pursuit and ride back to relieve him. By nightfall the Persian Empire belonged to a 25-year-old Macedonian.

annotations.text: Darius is murdered the next year by his own satraps. Alexander takes his throne, his treasury, and his title.

hastings-1066.title: Hastings: The Feigned Retreat
hastings-1066.intro: October 14, 1066. Harold Godwinson's exhausted Anglo-Saxon army, fresh from a 250-mile forced march, takes a defensive position on Senlac Hill against William the Conqueror's invasion force. The day ends with Harold dead and England changed forever.
hastings-1066.battlefieldDesc: Senlac Hill near Hastings, Anglo-Saxon shield wall on the ridge, Normans below.

phases.title: The Shield Wall
phases.narration: Harold's housecarls form a shield wall on the crest of Senlac Hill, with fyrd militia behind. William deploys below in three lines: archers in front, infantry behind, cavalry in reserve.

phases.title: The Norman Assault
phases.narration: Norman archers fire uphill, arrows stick in shields. Norman infantry charges and breaks against the wall. William's heavy cavalry follows, but men and horses are repulsed back down the slope.

phases.title: The Breton Rout
phases.narration: On the Norman left, the Bretons break in a real retreat. The English right wing, smelling victory, charges down the hill in pursuit, breaking the shield wall.

phases.title: William's Counter
phases.narration: William rallies the Normans, wheels his cavalry into the pursuing English on the open ground, and cuts them off from the hill. The pursuing fyrd are slaughtered in detail. The shield wall, now with a gap, never recovers fully.

phases.title: The Feigned Retreats
phases.narration: Having seen what real retreats can do, William orders feigned retreats. Twice more, sections of his line pretend to break. Twice more, English troops descend the hill, and are cut to pieces in the open.

phases.title: Arrows and an Eye
phases.narration: Norman archers fire high, dropping arrows behind the shield wall onto the fyrd. Tradition says one strikes Harold in the eye. With their king dead, the wall collapses. England falls to a duke from Normandy.

agincourt-1415.title: Agincourt: Mud and the Longbow
agincourt-1415.intro: October 25, 1415. A small, hungry, dysentery-ridden English army under Henry V is trapped by a French force three to five times its size. The French expect a chivalric massacre. The English have longbows, mud, and a narrow field.
agincourt-1415.battlefieldDesc: Plowed field between two woods, Agincourt, a funnel ~750m wide, ankle-deep in mud.

phases.title: The Funnel
phases.narration: Henry positions his army between two thick woods that narrow the killing ground. Longbowmen flank his men-at-arms. Sharpened stakes are driven into the ground in front. The French, in three vast lines, fill the whole far end.

units.label: French first line, knights on foot

phases.title: Provocation
phases.narration: After hours of standoff, Henry advances within longbow range and replants his stakes. The first English arrow storm strikes the front of the French line, killing horses and goading the French into action.

phases.title: The Mud
phases.narration: French heavy cavalry charges the longbowmen. Stakes and arrows shred the horses. Crippled horses fall into the plowed mud. The first French line of dismounted knights, in 70 pounds of plate, slogs forward, and the field becomes a swamp.

phases.title: Bowmen Out of Arrows
phases.narration: When the French first line finally reaches the English, exhausted, English men-at-arms fight them to a standstill while longbowmen pull mallets, hatchets, and daggers and attack the flanks. The French second line, pressed forward by the men behind, crushes its own first line.

phases.title: The Slaughter and the Prisoners
phases.narration: Heaps of French dead and dying pile up. Thousands surrender. When Henry hears rumors of a fresh French attack, he orders the prisoners killed, a still-debated decision. The third French line declines to attack. Six thousand French dead. Maybe four hundred English.

annotations.text: "We few, we happy few, we band of brothers", Shakespeare, two centuries later.

trafalgar-1805.title: Trafalgar: Nelson's Two Columns
trafalgar-1805.intro: October 21, 1805. Off Cape Trafalgar, 27 British ships of the line under Nelson meet 33 French and Spanish under Villeneuve. The conventional doctrine is parallel lines and a slow exchange of broadsides. Nelson does something else.
trafalgar-1805.battlefieldDesc: Atlantic Ocean off Cape Trafalgar, Spain. Light winds, heavy swell.

phases.title: The Lines
phases.narration: Villeneuve's combined fleet is strung out in a long, curving line sailing north. Nelson approaches in two columns at right angles, aiming to cut the enemy line into three pieces and overwhelm the leeward portion before the windward ships can return.

phases.title: Approach Under Fire
phases.narration: The British close perpendicular to the enemy at three knots. For an hour the French and Spanish rake them, broadsides crashing into Nelson's lead ships with no British return fire possible. Sailors lie flat on the decks.

phases.title: Cutting the Line
phases.narration: Victory passes astern of Villeneuve's Bucentaure, firing a triple-shotted broadside down the length of the French flagship. Collingwood's Royal Sovereign cuts through the rear, the British line piercing the Franco-Spanish line at two places.

phases.title: Pell-Mell Battle
phases.narration: Nelson's plan trades formation for chaos. British gun crews fire two to three times faster than Franco-Spanish gun crews. Ship-on-ship duels at point-blank range. Aboard Victory, Nelson is struck by a sniper from the rigging of Redoutable.

annotations.text: Nelson, mortally wounded, lives long enough to hear of his victory: 'Thank God I have done my duty.'

phases.title: Aftermath
phases.narration: By 5 PM the action is over. 22 Franco-Spanish ships are captured or sunk. No British ship is lost. A four-day gale then destroys most of the prizes. France's invasion of Britain is permanently shelved. The Royal Navy rules every ocean for a century.

austerlitz-1805.title: Austerlitz: The Pratzen Trap
austerlitz-1805.intro: December 2, 1805. On the anniversary of his coronation, Napoleon faces a combined Russian and Austrian army that outnumbers him 85,000 to 67,000. He deliberately abandons the strongest position on the field, the Pratzen Heights, to bait an attack he has already planned to break.
austerlitz-1805.battlefieldDesc: Plateau of Pratzen, central Moravia. Frozen ponds to the south, hills to the north.

phases.title: The Bait
phases.narration: Napoleon makes his right flank look weak and undefended. The Allies see the trap they think it is, a chance to roll up the French line, and pour the bulk of their army southward off the Pratzen Heights to attack Davout's small corps.

phases.title: The Allied Sweep South
phases.narration: Tsar Alexander overrules Kutuzov's caution. Russian and Austrian columns abandon the Pratzen Heights and march south to envelop Davout, weakening the very center on which their position depends.

phases.title: Soult Strikes the Heights
phases.narration: As the fog lifts off the Goldbach valley, Soult's IV Corps surges up the Pratzen slopes, into the abandoned center of the Allied position. "One sharp blow, and the war is over," Napoleon had said the night before. He had planned for this hour exactly.

phases.title: The Allied Center Split
phases.narration: French infantry tops the Pratzen Heights. The Allied army is now in two pieces, a strong wing trapped in the south, a weakened wing trapped in the north, and Napoleon stands between them with the Imperial Guard.

phases.title: The Ponds
phases.narration: The southern Allied wing, attacked from front and rear, breaks for the frozen Satschan ponds. French artillery cracks the ice. Hundreds, by some accounts thousands, drown. By dusk the Third Coalition has ceased to exist.

annotations.text: Napoleon: 'It is the finest evening of my life.' Holy Roman Empire dissolved within months.

waterloo-1815.title: Waterloo: The Last Day
waterloo-1815.intro: Napoleon Bonaparte escaped Elba in March 1815 and returned to the throne of France. The Seventh Coalition declared him an outlaw. By June he had an army of 198,000. He chose to strike the Anglo-Allied force in Belgium under Wellington and the Prussian army under Blücher before they could combine. On 16 June he beat Blücher at Ligny but did not destroy him. On 18 June he attacked Wellington at Mont-Saint-Jean. By midnight the Empire was over.
waterloo-1815.battlefieldDesc: South of Brussels, just south of the village of Waterloo. The battle is fought across a shallow valley between two parallel ridges, with three fortified positions on the floor: the Hougoumont farm complex on the right, the La Haye Sainte farm in the center, and the village of Plancenoit and the Papelotte farm on the left.

phases.title: The Morning
phases.narration: Heavy rain has soaked the ground overnight. Napoleon delays his attack to let the field dry so his artillery can recoil on firm earth. From La Belle-Alliance he can see Wellington's line on the Mont-Saint-Jean ridge. He has 73,000 men and 250 guns. Wellington has 68,000 of mixed British, Dutch-Belgian, and German troops. The Prussians under Blücher, beaten two days earlier at Ligny, are marching from Wavre. Napoleon believes he has hours before they arrive. He has fewer.

phases.title: Hougoumont
phases.narration: Napoleon opens the battle with a diversionary attack on Hougoumont, the walled farmhouse anchoring Wellington's right. Prince Jerome Bonaparte takes the attack personally and turns the diversion into a meatgrinder. Two French divisions are eventually drawn into the assault. The British Coldstream Guards and Scots Guards hold the chateau and garden through the day. The North Gate breach by Lieutenant Legros is sealed by Sergeant James Graham and a handful of Coldstreamers, a moment Wellington later said decided the battle.

phases.title: D'Erlon Attacks the Center
phases.narration: After an 80-gun preparatory bombardment Napoleon sends D'Erlon's four divisions, 14,000 men in dense formation, against Wellington's center east of La Haye Sainte. Picton's 5th Division meets them at the crest. Picton is killed by a musket ball to the forehead. Bylandt's Dutch brigade breaks under massed fire. The center is starting to give.

phases.title: Union and Household Cavalry Charge
phases.narration: Uxbridge unleashes the two heavy cavalry brigades. The Household Brigade (Life Guards, Royal Horse Guards, 1st Dragoon Guards) and the Union Brigade (Royals, Scots Greys, Inniskillings) ride into D'Erlon's columns and scatter them. Sergeant Charles Ewart of the Scots Greys captures the eagle of the 45th Ligne. The British cavalry pursue too far, ride into French lancers, and lose nearly half their strength. The shock breaks D'Erlon's attack but spends Wellington's heavy cavalry for the day.

phases.title: Ney's Cavalry Charges
phases.narration: Marshal Michel Ney, the bravest of the brave, mistakes a Wellington tactical adjustment for a retreat. He launches wave after wave of cuirassiers and lancers, ultimately 9,000 horsemen, at the unbroken Anglo-Allied infantry. The British and German infantry form squares. The French cavalry sweeps between the squares, can do nothing to them, and retreats every time under canister and volley fire. Ney has two horses shot from under him. He commits no infantry support and no horse artillery. The charges achieve nothing and burn an hour and a half.

phases.title: La Haye Sainte Falls
phases.narration: The King's German Legion under Major George Baring runs out of ammunition in La Haye Sainte. Ney's infantry finally take the farm and bring up horse artillery onto the open rise behind it. Their canister fire tears into the British and German line at 300 yards. Wellington's center is punctured. He sends every uncommitted reserve forward. Wellington is heard to mutter, 'Night or the Prussians must come.'

movements.label: Final assault on La Haye Sainte

phases.title: Prussians at Plancenoit
phases.narration: Blücher's IV Corps under Bülow emerges from the Bois de Paris on Napoleon's right flank. They take the village of Plancenoit. Napoleon detaches Lobau's VI Corps and then two battalions of the Young Guard and finally two battalions of the Old Guard to retake it. The fight at Plancenoit consumes Napoleon's reserves the moment he most needs them. Grouchy, with 33,000 men sent after a phantom, is fighting the wrong Prussian corps at Wavre and never arrives.

phases.title: La Garde Recule
phases.narration: Napoleon commits the Middle Guard, four battalions in two columns, against Wellington's center-right. The columns are ravaged by the Royal Horse Artillery as they climb the muddy slope. At the crest the 1st Foot Guards rise from concealment behind the ridge and pour volleys into the lead column. The 52nd Light Infantry under John Colborne wheels to take the second column in the flank. The Guard recoils. Down the line French infantry see the impossible and cry 'La Garde recule!' The army's morale collapses.

phases.title: Sauve Qui Peut
phases.narration: Wellington stands in his stirrups, raises his hat, and waves the line forward. The Anglo-Allied army, with the Prussians driving in from the east, sweeps off the ridge and rolls up the French line. The Old Guard battalions around La Belle-Alliance form squares and march off in good order, the legendary 'La Garde meurt et ne se rend pas.' Around them the rest of the army dissolves. Cambronne is wounded and captured. Napoleon flees toward Paris. Blücher and Wellington meet at La Belle-Alliance in the dark.

gettysburg-1863.title: Gettysburg: Three Days on a Fishhook
gettysburg-1863.intro: 1 July 1863. The Army of Northern Virginia under Robert E. Lee has crossed the Potomac on a second invasion of the North. The Army of the Potomac, just handed to George G. Meade three days earlier, races to intercept. The armies collide at a Pennsylvania crossroads town where ten roads meet, and over three days fight the largest battle ever waged in the Western Hemisphere. The Confederacy will never invade the North again.
gettysburg-1863.battlefieldDesc: Adams County, Pennsylvania. A small town surrounded by farms and ridges. The Confederate line forms along Seminary Ridge to the west. The Union line forms a fishhook shape, anchored at Culp's Hill in the north, bending around Cemetery Hill, and running south down Cemetery Ridge to Little Round Top and Big Round Top.

phases.title: Buford on the Ridge
phases.narration: Brigadier General John Buford's two cavalry brigades arrive in Gettysburg the evening before the battle and recognize the value of the ridges south of town. Dismounted at Herr Ridge and McPherson Ridge, the troopers fight on foot with Sharps and Spencer carbines against Henry Heth's Confederate infantry division advancing from Cashtown. Buford's stand buys time for John Reynolds' I Corps to double-time up from Emmitsburg.

phases.title: Reynolds Killed
phases.narration: Reynolds arrives at the head of the Iron Brigade and orders Wisconsin and Michigan regiments into Herbst Woods at the double-quick. Within minutes a Confederate marksman shoots him out of the saddle. The Iron Brigade traps and captures James J. Archer's brigade, the first Confederate general officer taken in the war. Doubleday assumes command and holds McPherson Ridge into the afternoon.

phases.title: Collapse at Oak Ridge and Barlow's Knoll
phases.narration: The Confederate II Corps under Richard Ewell arrives from the north, Rodes from Carlisle and Early from York. They find the Union XI Corps under Howard already deployed but the line is too long and too thin. Francis Barlow's division occupies a forward knoll without orders, a position later called Barlow's Knoll. Early's veterans flank it from three sides. The XI Corps collapses and streams back through the streets of Gettysburg in scenes that recall Chancellorsville two months earlier.

phases.title: The Fishhook Forms
phases.narration: Winfield Hancock arrives on Cemetery Hill with orders from Meade to assess the ground. He recommends staying. Through the night the Army of the Potomac files into a position shaped like a fishhook: the barb at Culp's Hill, the bend at Cemetery Hill, the shank south down Cemetery Ridge to the Round Tops. Lee orders Ewell to take Cemetery Hill if practicable. Ewell does not press the attack. By morning every approach is held in strength.

phases.title: Longstreet's Long March
phases.narration: Lee's plan for the second day is an attack en echelon up the Emmitsburg Road, with James Longstreet's I Corps rolling up the Union left. Longstreet, who disagrees with the assault, takes most of the morning to position his men. Daniel Sickles's III Corps, on the Union left, has already moved a half mile forward to higher ground at the Peach Orchard, leaving Little Round Top almost undefended.

phases.title: Little Round Top
phases.narration: Gouverneur K. Warren, Meade's chief engineer, climbs Little Round Top, sees that it is undefended, and grabs the first brigade he can find: Strong Vincent's, including the 20th Maine under Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain. They reach the summit minutes before the 15th and 47th Alabama. After an hour of point-blank fighting and out of ammunition, Chamberlain orders a downhill bayonet charge. The Alabama regiments break. The Union left holds.

phases.title: Devil's Den, Wheatfield, Peach Orchard
phases.narration: Hood is wounded in the arm by an air-burst at the start of the assault. Texas and Alabama regiments take Devil's Den from de Trobriand's brigade. The 20-acre Wheatfield changes hands six times in two hours. McLaws breaks Sickles's salient at the Peach Orchard and rolls it up the Emmitsburg Road, but the Union line stiffens along Plum Run as Hancock feeds in reserves from II Corps.

phases.title: Culp's Hill at Night
phases.narration: Edward Johnson's CSA division attacks Culp's Hill at dusk. Most of Slocum's XII Corps has been pulled out to shore up the Union left. George Greene's lone brigade of New Yorkers holds the breastworks on the upper hill. They are outnumbered five to one but the breastworks save them. Confederate brigades occupy abandoned Union positions on the lower hill in the dark and dig in for the morning.

phases.title: The Great Cannonade
phases.narration: Lee plans a frontal assault on the Union center. Edward Porter Alexander masses 150 to 170 Confederate guns along Seminary Ridge and opens fire on the Union II Corps position. The Union artillery, 80 to 90 guns under Henry Hunt, replies. The barrage is the largest of the war in North America and audible 200 miles away in Pittsburgh. Most of the Confederate shells overshoot. Hunt orders his guns silent to conserve ammunition and to draw the assault.

phases.title: Pickett's Charge
phases.narration: 12,500 Confederates of Pickett's, Pettigrew's, and Trimble's divisions step off from the woods on Seminary Ridge and march three quarters of a mile across open ground toward the Union center. Union artillery and rifle fire from the Angle and from Cemetery Ridge tear gaps in the lines. About 200 Virginians under Lewis Armistead breach the Union line at the copse of trees. Armistead falls mortally wounded with his hand on a Union gun. The high water mark of the Confederacy lasts five minutes.

phases.title: Lee Retreats
phases.narration: Lee withdraws toward Virginia on the night of 4 July, the wagon train of his wounded stretching 17 miles. Meade does not pursue aggressively. Heavy rains swell the Potomac and Lee is trapped against the river for ten days at Williamsport. He crosses the Potomac on the night of 13 to 14 July. The Army of Northern Virginia loses about 28,000 of 75,000 engaged. The Army of the Potomac loses about 23,000 of 93,000. Vicksburg falls to Grant on the same day the high water recedes from Cemetery Ridge. The Confederacy will fight for almost two more years but never again invade the North.

stalingrad-1942.title: Stalingrad: The City That Did Not Fall
stalingrad-1942.intro: August 1942. Hitler has split Army Group South in two and sent half of it, the 6th Army and the 4th Panzer Army, the cream of the Wehrmacht, to take Stalingrad. The city is to be the German anchor on the Volga, the steel cap to the southern flank of the Eastern Front. Six months later, after two and a half million casualties on both sides, the 6th Army surrenders in the basement of a department store and the Wehrmacht never advances on the Eastern Front again.
stalingrad-1942.battlefieldDesc: A 50-km strip of city along the western bank of the Volga, ringed on the west by 250 km of open steppe. The city itself runs north-south for 30 km between the Tractor Factory complex in the north and the grain elevator in the south.

phases.title: Drive to the Volga
phases.narration: Friedrich Paulus's 6th Army and Hermann Hoth's 4th Panzer Army drive across the Don steppe toward the Volga. By 23 August the 16th Panzer Division reaches the Volga north of Stalingrad. The Luftwaffe levels the city in a single afternoon with 1,000 sorties , 40,000 civilians die. Stalin forbids evacuation of the population: 'We will defend the city to which the Leader has given his name.'

phases.title: The City Burns
phases.narration: Vasily Chuikov takes command of the 62nd Army on 12 September with orders to hold what cannot be held. His tactic: 'hug the enemy.' Soviet infantry stay so close to the Germans that the Luftwaffe and German artillery cannot fire without hitting their own. Every house, every floor, every staircase becomes a battlefield. Pavlov's House, defended for 58 days by 25 men, appears on operational maps in Hitler's headquarters as a major German objective.

phases.title: The Factories
phases.narration: Paulus throws three fresh divisions at the northern factory district. Fighting reaches the assembly line of the Tractor Factory, workers weld the last T-34s and drive them straight from the factory floor into combat. The Barrikady gun plant changes hands seven times. Yet across the Volga the Stavka is already moving the armies for something else entirely.

phases.title: Uranus, The Pincers
phases.narration: Zhukov, Vasilevsky, and Vatutin have spent two months assembling 1.1 million men, 14,000 guns, and 900 tanks on the flanks of the Stalingrad bulge, held by Romanian, Hungarian, and Italian armies. At 07:20 on 19 November, 3,500 guns open up against the Romanian 3rd Army at Serafimovich. The Romanians break by noon. The next morning, the southern arm, 51st and 57th Armies, hits the Romanian 4th Army south of the city. Both flanks collapse.

phases.title: Linkup at Kalach
phases.narration: Four days after Uranus opens, the 4th Tank Corps from the north and the 4th Mechanized Corps from the south meet at Sovetsky village just east of Kalach-na-Donu. ~290,000 men of Paulus's 6th Army and elements of the 4th Panzer are trapped in a 50-km-wide pocket east of the Don. Hitler orders Paulus to hold, Göring promises 500 tons of supply per day by air. The Luftwaffe will deliver less than 100 on most days.

phases.title: Wintergewitter, Manstein's Relief
phases.narration: Erich von Manstein launches Operation Winter Storm, the LVII Panzer Corps under Hoth strikes north from Kotelnikovo toward the pocket. On the 19th, Hoth's 6th Panzer reaches the Myshkova River, 48 km from Paulus's perimeter. Paulus has fuel for one of two options: break out south, or stay and defend the city. He chooses to stay. Manstein has no reserves and the Soviets are already counterattacking his flanks. On the 23rd he calls off the relief.

phases.title: Saturn and the Italian Collapse
phases.narration: While Manstein's relief stalls, the Stavka launches Little Saturn against the Italian 8th Army holding the middle Don. The Italians fight better than Hitler's headquarters expected, but they have no anti-tank weapons that can stop T-34s, and they break. Soviet armor reaches Tatsinskaya airfield, where the Luftwaffe is staging supply runs to Stalingrad. 50 Ju-52s are destroyed on the ground.

phases.title: Pitomnik
phases.narration: The pocket shrinks under Soviet pressure from every side. Rokossovsky's Don Front opens Operation Ring on 10 January with 5,000 guns. Pitomnik, the larger of two airfields in the pocket, falls on the 16th. Gumrak holds for six more days. After Gumrak there is no way in or out, the wounded who walk to the airfield die on the runway. Soviet pressure forces Paulus's headquarters to relocate three times in two weeks.

phases.title: Paulus Surrenders the South
phases.narration: On 30 January, the tenth anniversary of Hitler's chancellorship, the Führer promotes Paulus to Field Marshal, no German field marshal had ever surrendered. The message is unmistakable: die fighting or kill yourself. The next morning Soviet soldiers enter the basement of the Univermag department store where the 6th Army headquarters has retreated. Paulus surrenders. Hitler: 'They have surrendered there, formally and absolutely. Otherwise they would have closed ranks, formed a hedgehog, and shot themselves with their last bullet.'

phases.title: The Northern Pocket Yields
phases.narration: The northern pocket, XI Corps under Karl Strecker, holds out two more days in the wreckage of the Tractor Factory. At 14:00 on the 2nd of February, Strecker radios the OKW: 'XI Corps and its six divisions have done their duty. Long live Germany!' Then he stops the radios. ~91,000 Germans surrender, including 22 generals. Of those who march east, only ~5,000 will see Germany again.

midway-1942.title: Midway: Five Minutes
midway-1942.intro: Six months after Pearl Harbor, Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto sails the strongest carrier force in history toward Midway atoll, hoping to draw the last American carriers into a fight he can win. He has the ships, the planes, and the pilots. Code-breakers in Honolulu, working with a tipped-off Pacific Fleet commander named Chester Nimitz, will give the Americans the one thing the Japanese cannot: knowing exactly where the enemy will be, and when.
midway-1942.battlefieldDesc: Open Pacific Ocean around Midway atoll, roughly 32 degrees north, 178 degrees west. The closest land for hundreds of miles is the atoll itself. The fight is fought entirely by carrier aircraft over distances of 150 to 250 miles.

phases.title: Yamamoto's Plan
phases.narration: Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto's plan is to draw out the remaining US carriers and finish what Pearl Harbor started. The First Air Fleet, four heavy carriers under Vice Admiral Chuichi Nagumo, is to bomb Midway atoll into compliance. A separate invasion force will then land. American carriers are expected to sortie from Pearl, where they will be destroyed in detail by the carriers, by submarines, and by Yamamoto's battleships steaming behind. What the Japanese do not know is that Joseph Rochefort's HYPO station broke their JN-25 naval code in May.

phases.title: First Strike on Midway
phases.narration: 108 Japanese aircraft hit Midway. The Marine fighter squadron VMF-221, flying obsolete Buffaloes, is shredded. Most of the atoll's surface installations burn. Strike leader Joichi Tomonaga radios Nagumo that a second strike will be needed to soften Midway further. Nagumo orders his reserve aircraft, the planes armed with torpedoes for ships, to switch their weapons for bombs to hit Midway. This rearmament order will kill him.

phases.title: Midway Hits Back
phases.narration: Midway-based aircraft attack the Japanese carriers across the morning. Six TBF Avengers and four B-26 Marauders score no hits and lose seven planes. Sixteen Marine SBDs of VMSB-241 score no hits. Fifteen B-17s drop from 20,000 feet and score no hits, though their crews report otherwise. None of these attacks damage a Japanese ship. They do force Nagumo's air groups to remain on combat air patrol over the fleet and out of the rearmament cycle.

phases.title: Nagumo Rearms Twice
phases.narration: Scout plane Tone Number 4 finally reports an American carrier at 08:20. Nagumo now faces a choice. His decks are covered in planes being switched from torpedoes to bombs for a second Midway strike, with fuel hoses and ordnance scattered across the hangars. He orders another switch back to anti-ship weapons. The crews try to comply while under continuous attack from Midway-based planes and US carrier torpedo bombers. By 10:20 the four Japanese flight decks are vulnerable masses of fuel and ordnance.

phases.title: Torpedo Eight
phases.narration: Torpedo Squadron 8 from USS Hornet, fifteen TBD Devastators under Lieutenant Commander John C. Waldron, finds the Japanese fleet without their own fighter escort. Waldron leads them in at wave-top height into a wall of Zero fighters and anti-aircraft fire. Every Devastator is shot down. Only Ensign George Gay survives, treading water under his seat cushion. Within an hour Torpedo 6 from Enterprise and Torpedo 3 from Yorktown attack in turn. Of the 41 Devastators that take off, 35 do not return. None score a hit. They do hold the Japanese CAP at low altitude.

phases.title: The Five Minutes
phases.narration: Lieutenant Commander Wade McClusky leads thirty-two SBD Dauntless dive bombers from Enterprise. His squadrons are low on fuel and lost. He spots the wake of a Japanese destroyer, the Arashi, racing northeast after attacking the submarine USS Nautilus. McClusky follows it. The destroyer leads him straight to Nagumo's carriers. At 10:22, McClusky's bombers and Max Leslie's from Yorktown roll in on Akagi, Kaga, and Soryu. The Japanese CAP is still at low altitude. Within five minutes three of the four Japanese carriers are burning wrecks.

phases.title: Hiryu Strikes Back
phases.narration: Hiryu, the last surviving Japanese carrier, launches two strikes against Yorktown across the afternoon. The first, eighteen Vals under Lieutenant Michio Kobayashi, plants three bombs into Yorktown that the damage control parties manage to suppress. The second, ten Kates under Lieutenant Joichi Tomonaga, puts two torpedoes into Yorktown's port side. The carrier lists 26 degrees and Admiral Fletcher orders her abandoned at 14:55.

phases.title: Hiryu Killed
phases.narration: Spruance, now in tactical command, sends the last available Dauntlesses against Hiryu. Twenty-four SBDs from Enterprise and Yorktown (operating off Enterprise) find Hiryu at 17:00. Four 1,000-pound bombs hit, the flight deck buckles, and Hiryu burns through the night. Admiral Tamon Yamaguchi remains aboard and is lost with the ship in the early hours of 5 June. With all four Japanese fleet carriers gone, Yamamoto cancels the invasion and turns west.

phases.title: Yorktown Sunk
phases.narration: Yorktown is taken under tow by the destroyer Hammann. Damage control parties reboard and have her listing back upright when the Japanese submarine I-168 fires four torpedoes on the morning of 6 June. Two hit Yorktown, one hits Hammann, one runs under both ships. Hammann sinks in four minutes. Yorktown rolls over and sinks at dawn on 7 June. She is the last American carrier loss of the battle.

phases.title: Turn of the Pacific War
phases.narration: The Japanese lose four heavy carriers, the cruiser Mikuma, 248 aircraft, and about 3,057 men, including roughly 110 trained naval aviators. The United States loses Yorktown, Hammann, about 150 aircraft, and 307 men. The strategic balance reverses inside a single morning. The Imperial Navy will never again take the offensive in the Central Pacific. The road to Tokyo runs through Guadalcanal, Tarawa, Saipan, Iwo Jima, and Okinawa.

thermopylae-480bc.title: Thermopylae: The Hot Gates
thermopylae-480bc.intro: August 480 BC. Xerxes's army, perhaps 100,000 effectives, marches south into Greece. At a narrow coastal pass, 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians, 400 Thebans, and a few thousand allied Greeks block the road. The plan is to hold for time. The cost is everyone who stays.
thermopylae-480bc.battlefieldDesc: Coastal pass between Mt. Kallidromo and the Malian Gulf, fifteen meters wide at the narrowest.

phases.title: The Pass
phases.narration: Leonidas anchors the Greek line in the West Gate, the narrowest of three chokepoints, with the Phocian wall behind. Persian numbers cannot be brought to bear: only a few dozen men can engage at a time. The sea covers the right flank. Sheer cliffs cover the left.

phases.title: Day One, Medes Repulsed
phases.narration: Xerxes orders Median troops to take the pass. Wave after wave breaks against the Greek phalanx, which absorbs the attack and pushes back. The shallow front lets Greek heavy spears do their work. Persian short stabbing weapons cannot reach.

phases.title: Day Two, The Immortals Try
phases.narration: Xerxes sends his Immortals, Persia's elite household troops. The result is the same. Greek formations rotate in shifts so fresh men are always at the spearpoint. Persian casualties mount. Greek losses are still light.

phases.title: Betrayal, The Anopaea Path
phases.narration: A local named Ephialtes shows the Persians the Anopaea, a goat track over the mountains that bypasses the pass. The Immortals are ordered to take it overnight. The 1,000 Phocians guarding the path are surprised and routed.

phases.title: The Last Stand
phases.narration: Learning he has been outflanked, Leonidas dismisses most of the allied contingents to fight another day. He keeps the 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians who refuse to leave, and 400 Thebans. They advance into the wider part of the pass, take the Persians by surprise, and fight until almost no one is left standing.

annotations.text: Inscription at the site: "Go tell the Spartans, passer-by, that here, obedient to their laws, we lie."

salamis-480bc.title: Salamis: The Narrow Strait
salamis-480bc.intro: September 480 BC. After Thermopylae, Xerxes has burned Athens. The Greek fleet, outnumbered roughly two-to-one, has fallen back to the strait between Salamis and the mainland. Themistocles convinces the Persian king to attack into water too narrow for his numbers to matter.
salamis-480bc.battlefieldDesc: Strait of Salamis, narrow channel between Salamis island and Attica.

phases.title: The Lure
phases.narration: A messenger from Themistocles tells Xerxes the Greeks are about to flee. The Persian fleet rows all night to seal both ends of the strait. Crews are exhausted by dawn.

phases.title: The Persian Advance
phases.narration: The Persian fleet rows west into the narrowing strait. Three lines deep, they cannot maneuver. Front ranks block back ranks. The water tightens.

phases.title: The Greek Strike
phases.narration: Greek triremes, heavier, with bronze rams, backwater briefly to lure the Persians further, then strike. In the crush, Persian ships cannot turn. Greek rams crack hulls. Oars splinter. Persian rowers drown in armor.

phases.title: The Rout
phases.narration: Disordered, captains lose their nerve. Persian ships flee east, ramming each other in the panic. Greeks pursue. Aristides lands hoplites on Psyttaleia island and kills the marines Xerxes had stationed there to slaughter Greek survivors.

annotations.text: Xerxes watches from a throne on Mt. Aegaleos. Within weeks he withdraws to Asia, leaving his army stranded in Greece.

alesia-52bc.title: Alesia: The Double Siege
alesia-52bc.intro: September 52 BC. Vercingetorix has retreated his 80,000-strong Gallic army into the hilltop fortress of Alesia. Caesar arrives with 50,000 Romans and does something audacious: rather than storm the walls, he encircles the fortress with siegeworks, and then builds a second wall facing outward, expecting a relief army.
alesia-52bc.battlefieldDesc: Hilltop oppidum of Alesia, central Gaul. Caesar's circumvallation (inner ring) and contravallation (outer ring).

phases.title: Vercingetorix Retreats to the Hill
phases.narration: After a cavalry defeat in open country, Vercingetorix takes his army into Alesia, a defensible plateau ringed by valleys. He expects Caesar to either storm the walls (impossible) or starve out the defenders (slow). He sends riders for relief.

phases.title: Circumvallation
phases.narration: Roman engineers build an 11-mile inner ring of trenches, walls, towers, and traps facing inward at Alesia. Vercingetorix attempts sorties to disrupt the work. Each is repulsed. Inside the oppidum, food runs out. He expels women, children, and the elderly to save rations, Caesar refuses to let them pass through Roman lines.

phases.title: The Relief Army Appears
phases.narration: A Gallic relief army, some 250,000 men levied from across Gaul under Commius, arrives behind the Roman besiegers. Caesar is now between two armies, each potentially larger than his. He completes the contravallation, a 13-mile outer wall facing outward, just in time.

phases.title: Two-Front Assault
phases.narration: The relief army strikes the outer wall while Vercingetorix sorties against the inner wall. Romans defend both sides simultaneously. The fighting is the hardest of the Gallic Wars, both walls nearly breached. Caesar himself rides between threatened points wearing his red cloak so legionaries can see him.

phases.title: The Cavalry Decision
phases.narration: At the most critical moment, Caesar leads his reserve cavalry around the entire siege complex and falls on the rear of the relief army. The Gauls are now sandwiched. Their assault collapses. They flee. Watching from the walls, Vercingetorix knows he is finished.

phases.title: Surrender
phases.narration: Vercingetorix rides out of Alesia, dismounts, places his weapons at Caesar's feet, and sits in silence. He is taken to Rome, paraded in triumph six years later, and executed. Gaul becomes a Roman province for the next 400 years.

annotations.text: Caesar's account of the campaign, Commentarii de Bello Gallico, is still read in Latin classrooms today.

constantinople-1453.title: Fall of Constantinople
constantinople-1453.intro: Spring 1453. Constantinople, capital of the eastern Roman empire for 1,100 years, is defended by perhaps 7,000 men. Outside the walls, Sultan Mehmed II has 80,000 soldiers and a brand new weapon: cannons so large they have to be cast at the siege site. He intends to take the city. He does.
constantinople-1453.battlefieldDesc: Triple Theodosian walls of Constantinople. The Golden Horn to the north, Sea of Marmara to the south.

phases.title: The Walls
phases.narration: Constantinople's land walls, three lines, with moat, have not been breached in a thousand years. Constantine XI commands the defenders, including 700 Genoese under Giovanni Giustiniani. Mehmed deploys his army across the four-mile land front. His fleet blockades the Sea of Marmara.

phases.title: Urban's Great Cannon
phases.narration: The Hungarian engineer Orban, having offered his services to Constantine, then to Mehmed when Constantine couldn't pay, has cast a cannon 27 feet long firing 1,200-pound stone balls. It can be fired only three times a day, but its hits crack what arrows and ladders could not.

phases.title: Ships Over Land
phases.narration: A massive chain across the Golden Horn keeps Ottoman ships out of the city's harbor side. Mehmed has 70 of his galleys hauled overland on greased logs across a hill to bypass the chain and enter the Horn from above. The defenders, attacked from a new direction, must thin the land walls.

phases.title: The Final Assault
phases.narration: Mehmed launches a coordinated assault in three waves: irregulars first to exhaust the defenders, then Anatolian regulars, finally the Janissaries. Giustiniani is wounded and carried off. Defenders falter. A small gate, the Kerkoporta, is found unlocked. Ottomans pour through.

phases.title: The Last Emperor
phases.narration: Constantine XI removes his imperial insignia and disappears into the fighting. His body is never identified with certainty. By noon, Mehmed enters the city, the youngest Roman emperor in history at 21, and prays in Hagia Sophia, now a mosque.

annotations.text: The Eastern Roman Empire ends after 1,123 years. Greek scholars flee west to Italy, accelerating the Renaissance.

spanish-armada-1588.title: The Spanish Armada
spanish-armada-1588.intro: Summer 1588. Philip II of Spain sends 130 ships and 30,000 men to escort an invasion army from Flanders to England, depose Elizabeth, and return England to Catholicism. The English fleet, smaller and lighter, refuses to fight on Spanish terms. The Channel becomes a running gunfight for ten days.
spanish-armada-1588.battlefieldDesc: English Channel, from the Lizard in Cornwall east to Calais, then north past Scotland.

phases.title: Crescent Off the Lizard
phases.narration: The Armada sails up the Channel in a crescent formation, fighting ships on the wings, transports protected in the middle. The English fleet under Howard and Drake slips behind them, gaining the weather gauge: the wind position from which to attack at will.

phases.title: Running Battle
phases.narration: For a week the fleets exchange long-range gunfire as they drift east along the Channel. English ships are faster and have heavier long-range guns. Spanish ships are built to grapple and board, and their guns reload slowly. Neither side scores a decisive blow.

phases.title: Fireships at Calais
phases.narration: The Armada anchors off Calais to coordinate with the army in Flanders, which has not arrived. The English send eight fireships into the anchored fleet at midnight. Spanish captains cut their cables to escape, and lose formation in the dark.

phases.title: Battle of Gravelines
phases.narration: With Spanish ships scattered and unable to reform, English galleons close to within musket range and pound them with broadsides for eight hours. Five Spanish ships are sunk or captured. Many more are crippled. English ammunition runs out near sunset.

phases.title: The Long Way Home
phases.narration: Unable to return through the Channel, the Spanish flag officer Medina Sidonia orders the surviving fleet north around Scotland and Ireland. North Atlantic storms wreck more than 25 ships on the Irish coast. Of 130 vessels that sailed, perhaps 65 return home. Of 30,000 men, perhaps half.

annotations.text: Naval power decisively shifts from Spain to England. Within a century, England begins building a worldwide empire.

saratoga-1777.title: Saratoga: The Turning Point
saratoga-1777.intro: September–October 1777. A British army under John Burgoyne marches south from Canada to cut New England off from the rest of the colonies. After two pitched battles in upstate New York, he surrenders 6,222 men and France enters the war.
saratoga-1777.battlefieldDesc: Forested hills above the Hudson River near Saratoga and Bemis Heights.

phases.title: The British Plan
phases.narration: Burgoyne descends from Canada with regulars, German auxiliaries, Loyalists, and Indigenous allies. A second column under Howe was supposed to come up from New York City to meet him, but Howe sails to Philadelphia instead. Burgoyne marches south alone through difficult country and stretches his supply lines thin.

phases.title: Freeman's Farm
phases.narration: Burgoyne pushes against the American left under Daniel Morgan and Benedict Arnold. Morgan's Virginia riflemen, firing from cover, pick off British officers at long range. Arnold leads aggressive counter-attacks until Gates, who dislikes him, orders him back to camp. The British hold the field but lose 600 men they cannot replace.

phases.title: The Trap Tightens
phases.narration: Burgoyne entrenches and waits for reinforcement from New York. None comes. New England militia stream in to join Gates, by early October the Americans outnumber the British two to one. Indigenous allies and Loyalists desert. Supplies run out.

phases.title: Bemis Heights
phases.narration: Burgoyne sends out 1,500 men to probe the American left. Morgan and Poor crush the British reconnaissance. Arnold, formally relieved of command, leaves his tent without orders and leads the assault on the Breymann redoubt, taking a leg wound at the spot now marked by a boot-shaped monument that lacks his name.

phases.title: Surrender
phases.narration: Burgoyne falls back to Saratoga and finds the path north already cut by Stark's New Hampshire militia. Surrounded, outnumbered, and out of food, he surrenders his army by the Convention of Saratoga. 6,222 British and German soldiers stack arms.

annotations.text: Six months later, France signs an alliance with the United States. The American Revolution becomes a global war.

trenton-1776.title: Trenton: Christmas Night
trenton-1776.intro: Christmas night, 1776. The Continental Army has lost New York and most of New Jersey. Enlistments expire on January 1. George Washington crosses an ice-jammed Delaware River in a freezing storm with 2,400 men and surprises a Hessian garrison sleeping off the holiday. The American cause is saved in 90 minutes.
trenton-1776.battlefieldDesc: Trenton, New Jersey. Two columns of Continental troops converge on a small town held by 1,500 Hessians.

phases.title: The Crossing
phases.narration: Three hours behind schedule because of ice, Washington's 2,400 men cross the Delaware in Durham boats commanded by Marblehead fishermen. Sleet and freezing rain make every step dangerous. Two men freeze to death on the march.

phases.title: Two Columns
phases.narration: Once across, Washington splits the army. Greene's column will take the high ground north of Trenton. Sullivan's will swing south along the river. Both must arrive simultaneously to seal off the town. Snow muffles their approach.

phases.title: The Attack
phases.narration: Washington's columns arrive simultaneously at the edges of Trenton. Hessians, ill from Christmas drinking, are still in their billets. Colonel Rall is asleep. American artillery opens fire down the main streets at point-blank range. Hessian formations cannot form in the cross-fire.

phases.title: Rall Down
phases.narration: Colonel Rall, finally alert and on horseback, tries to rally his troops in an apple orchard and is shot from his saddle, mortally wounded. The Hessian regiments, von Lossberg, Knyphausen, Rall, fall back into the orchard and surrender in pieces.

phases.title: What It Saved
phases.narration: Twenty-two Hessians dead, 83 wounded, 896 captured, against two Americans frozen on the march. More importantly, enlistments due to expire on December 31 are extended. A week later Washington wins again at Princeton. The Continental Army survives the winter.

annotations.text: Pulitzer-winning historian David Hackett Fischer: "a forgotten masterpiece of warfare."

first-marne-1914.title: First Marne: The Taxis of Paris
first-marne-1914.intro: September 1914. The Schlieffen Plan is working: German armies have swept through Belgium and northern France and are within thirty miles of Paris. Then Joffre, the unflappable French commander, spots a gap. French taxicabs carry six thousand reinforcements to the front overnight. The Germans, exhausted and uncoordinated, fall back.
first-marne-1914.battlefieldDesc: Marne River valley east of Paris. A gap opens between the German First and Second Armies.

phases.title: The Great Wheel
phases.narration: Following the Schlieffen Plan, German armies sweep through Belgium and into France in a vast wheel west of Paris. They aim to crush France in six weeks, then turn east to face Russia. By early September, Paris seems lost. The French government evacuates to Bordeaux.

phases.title: Kluck Turns Inward
phases.narration: Kluck's First Army, on the German right, turns inward east of Paris to pursue retreating French forces. This decision opens a 30-mile gap between his army and Bülow's Second Army on his left. Joffre's reconnaissance spots it. So does the Paris military governor, Gallieni.

phases.title: The Taxis
phases.narration: Gallieni commandeers 600 Paris taxis to ferry 6,000 French reservists from the city out to the front in two nights. The image will become legendary. Maunoury's 6th Army strikes Kluck's exposed right flank along the Ourcq, forcing Kluck to disengage from his pursuit and wheel back to meet it.

phases.title: Franchet d'Espèrey and the BEF Press the Gap
phases.narration: While Kluck is occupied at the Ourcq, the French 5th Army under "Desperate Frankie" Franchet d'Espèrey and the British Expeditionary Force push into the widening gap between Kluck and Bülow. By the 8th, BEF and French troops are streaming through the gap with German armies on either side, dangerously close to envelopment.

phases.title: The German Retreat
phases.narration: Moltke, two hundred miles away in Luxembourg and nearly unable to communicate with his armies, sends Lieutenant-Colonel Hentsch on a fact-finding tour. Hentsch, possibly without authority, orders both Kluck and Bülow to withdraw to the Aisne. The Schlieffen Plan dies. Germany cannot win a quick war.

annotations.text: Both sides dig in. The trench warfare of the Western Front begins and will not end until November 1918.

tannenberg-1914.title: Tannenberg: The Russian Steamroller Derails
tannenberg-1914.intro: August 1914. Two Russian armies invade East Prussia. The Germans, using interior lines, intercepted radio messages sent in the clear, and the railway network, destroy one army before turning on the other. Samsonov shoots himself in a forest. Hindenburg and Ludendorff become heroes.
tannenberg-1914.battlefieldDesc: Forests and lakes of East Prussia (modern northeastern Poland). Two Russian armies separated by the Masurian Lakes.

phases.title: Two Russian Armies
phases.narration: Rennenkampf's First Army and Samsonov's Second Army cross the East Prussian frontier from the north and south of the Masurian Lakes respectively. The plan calls for them to converge and crush the German Eighth Army between them. The two armies are 50 miles apart and cannot easily coordinate.

phases.title: Gumbinnen, and a Panic
phases.narration: Prittwitz attacks Rennenkampf at Gumbinnen and is bloodily checked. He panics, considers retreating behind the Vistula. Moltke replaces him with Paul von Hindenburg, a retired officer, and Erich Ludendorff, the hero of Liège. Their chief of staff is Max Hoffmann, who has been quietly planning what comes next for weeks.

phases.title: The Redeployment
phases.narration: Hoffmann's plan: leave a thin cavalry screen against Rennenkampf, then move every other German formation south by rail to engage Samsonov alone. Crucially, the Russians are transmitting movement orders in the clear, German intercept stations read them word for word.

phases.title: Envelopment
phases.narration: Outnumbered Germans pin Samsonov's center while two corps swing around both flanks. With no contact from Rennenkampf to his north, Samsonov pushes his center deeper, exactly into the closing trap. Roads become choked with retreating Russian columns.

phases.title: Annihilation
phases.narration: The pocket closes around three Russian corps. Samsonov, his army disintegrating, his communications with Rennenkampf nonexistent, walks into a forest and shoots himself rather than report to the Tsar. 92,000 Russian troops are captured. 30,000 are killed or wounded. The Germans take ten days to evacuate the prisoners.

annotations.text: Tsar Nicholas II receives news of Samsonov's death without comment. Hindenburg becomes the icon of German wartime stoicism. The Hindenburg-Ludendorff partnership effectively rules Germany by 1916.

pearl-harbor-1941.title: Pearl Harbor: The Day of Infamy
pearl-harbor-1941.intro: 7 December 1941. Six Japanese carriers, 230 miles north of Oahu, launch 353 aircraft against the US Pacific Fleet at anchor. Within two hours four battleships are on the bottom and the United States is at war.
pearl-harbor-1941.battlefieldDesc: Pearl Harbor and Oahu, Territory of Hawaii.

phases.title: Kido Butai
phases.narration: Nagumo's strike force, six carriers (Akagi, Kaga, Sōryū, Hiryū, Shōkaku, Zuikaku) plus escorts, has sailed in radio silence from the Kurile Islands. It is now 230 miles north of Oahu. The first wave begins launching at 0600.

phases.title: First Wave
phases.narration: 183 aircraft, torpedo bombers, dive bombers, and Zero fighters, break formation over Oahu. Torpedo bombers come in low over the harbor. Modified shallow-running torpedoes drop into water just 40 feet deep. Battleship Row is hit before most ships' crews realize anything is wrong.

phases.title: Battleship Row
phases.narration: USS Arizona's forward magazine takes a bomb through the deck and detonates, the explosion rips the ship in half and kills 1,177 men in seconds. USS Oklahoma is hit by multiple torpedoes and capsizes. USS West Virginia, California, and Nevada are heavily hit. USS Utah, taken for an aircraft carrier, is sunk on the far side.

movements.label: USS Nevada makes for the channel

phases.title: Second Wave
phases.narration: 170 aircraft of the second wave find a harbor already burning, anti-aircraft fire now intense, and few targets left undamaged on Battleship Row. They turn to the airfields at Hickam, Wheeler, Kaneohe, destroying or damaging 188 American aircraft, most caught lined up on the runways to deter sabotage.

phases.title: What Was Missed, and What Wasn't
phases.narration: Nagumo declines to launch a third strike against fuel storage, dry docks, and submarine pens. Yamamoto later calls this his greatest regret. The American carriers, Enterprise, Lexington, Saratoga, are by accident or design at sea, untouched. They will sink four Japanese carriers at Midway in six months.

annotations.text: Yamamoto, reportedly, on the news: "I fear all we have done is to awaken a sleeping giant and fill him with a terrible resolve." The line was popularized by Tora! Tora! Tora! and is not certainly his.

balaclava-1854.title: Balaclava: The Light Brigade
balaclava-1854.intro: 25 October 1854. A Russian attack threatens the Allied supply port at Balaclava during the siege of Sevastopol. Three episodes etch this battle into permanent memory: the Thin Red Line, the Charge of the Heavy Brigade, and the Charge of the Light Brigade, 670 men sent by a confused order into the wrong valley.
balaclava-1854.battlefieldDesc: Two valleys north of Balaclava harbour. Russian artillery anchors the high ground.

phases.title: The Russian Attack
phases.narration: General Liprandi advances 25,000 Russians from the east. Within an hour they have overrun a chain of Turkish redoubts on the Causeway Heights and captured nine guns. The road to the Allied supply base at Balaclava lies open.

phases.title: The Thin Red Line
phases.narration: Russian cavalry pours down toward Balaclava. The 93rd (Highland) Regiment, 500 men in a single line two ranks deep, Times correspondent Russell will write "that thin red streak tipped with a line of steel", holds its ground and stops the cavalry charge with disciplined volleys. Highlanders do not form square. They do not need to.

phases.title: The Heavy Brigade
phases.narration: Brigadier Scarlett's Heavy Brigade, 800 dragoons, sees a Russian cavalry force five times its size descending the Heights. Without orders, Scarlett wheels and charges uphill into the head of the column. Eight minutes of melee. The Russian cavalry breaks and falls back over the Causeway.

phases.title: The Order
phases.narration: Lord Raglan, atop a ridge with a panoramic view, sees Russians trying to drag away the captured Turkish guns. He orders the Light Brigade to prevent this. The order passes through Quartermaster-General Airey to Captain Nolan, who carries it to Lord Lucan in the valley below. Lucan asks: "What guns?" Nolan, exasperated, points with his arm toward the wrong guns, those at the head of the North Valley, ringed on three sides by Russian artillery.

phases.title: Into the Valley
phases.narration: 670 cavalrymen begin to trot down the North Valley toward the wrong guns. Captain Nolan, the only one who knows the intended target, gallops ahead waving, and is killed by a shell-burst before he can correct anything. Russian guns open from three sides at once. The brigade picks up to a canter, then a gallop, then a full charge.

phases.title: The Reckoning
phases.narration: The surviving cavalrymen reach the guns, sabre the gunners, and start back. Of 670 men, 110 are killed, 161 wounded, 57 taken prisoner, 375 horses dead. The whole event lasts 20 minutes. The French general Bosquet, watching from the heights: "C'est magnifique, mais ce n'est pas la guerre, c'est de la folie."

annotations.text: Tennyson, six weeks later: "Theirs not to make reply / Theirs not to reason why / Theirs but to do and die."

battle-of-france-1940.title: Battle of France: The Sickle Cut
battle-of-france-1940.intro: In May 1940 the Wehrmacht's Manstein Plan sends seven panzer divisions through the supposedly impassable Ardennes Forest. The Allies, anchored on the Maginot Line and the Belgian frontier, look the wrong way. In six weeks Western Europe falls.
battle-of-france-1940.battlefieldDesc: Northwest Europe, North Sea coast at top, Ardennes forest center, Maginot Line at the southeast anchor.

phases.title: Dyle Plan deployment
phases.narration: The Allied high command expects a repeat of 1914: a German right hook through Belgium. The best French and BEF divisions advance to the Dyle River line. The center, opposite the Ardennes, is held by reservist Second Army. The Maginot Line garrisons the south.

phases.title: Manstein's gambit
phases.narration: Army Group B invades the Low Countries on schedule, drawing the Allied reserve north. Behind them, Army Group A funnels through the Ardennes in a 100-kilometer column of tanks. Allied air recon misses it. The French assume the forest is impassable to armor.

phases.title: Sedan crossing
phases.narration: Guderian's XIX Panzer Corps reaches the Meuse at Sedan. Massed Stuka attacks paralyze French defenders. Combat engineers throw rafts across. Tanks follow on pontoon bridges by nightfall. The French Second Army's reservists break.

phases.title: Race to the Channel
phases.narration: Instead of swinging south for Paris, the panzer corps drive west, straight for the English Channel. They cover 350 kilometers in five days, slicing behind the best Allied armies in Belgium. Allied counterattacks at Arras briefly bloody Rommel's 7th Panzer but cannot close the gap.

units.label: French reserves south of the cut

phases.title: The Dunkirk pocket
phases.narration: The BEF and surviving French units fall back to a shrinking perimeter around Dunkirk. Hitler's halt order, letting the Luftwaffe finish the pocket rather than the panzers, buys time. Operation Dynamo lifts 338,226 troops to England in eight days, the army saved without its equipment.

annotations.text: Hitler's halt order: panzers pause 24–26 May. The British army escapes.

antietam-1862.title: Antietam: The Bloodiest Single Day
antietam-1862.intro: 17 September 1862. Lee's first invasion of the North hinges on a divided army facing a Union force twice its size on the banks of Antietam Creek. McClellan attacks in three uncoordinated thrusts. By nightfall over 22,000 Americans are dead, wounded, or missing, the bloodiest day in American history.
antietam-1862.battlefieldDesc: Antietam Creek flows south through gentle hills west of Sharpsburg, Maryland. Cornfield to the north, Sunken Road in the center, three stone bridges across the creek to the south.

phases.title: Dawn deployment
phases.narration: Lee anchors his line on Sharpsburg with his back to the Potomac, Jackson on the left near the Dunker Church, D.H. Hill in the center, Longstreet on the right above the lower bridge. McClellan has six corps to Lee's three divisions but he commits them piecemeal.

phases.title: The Cornfield
phases.narration: Hooker attacks south through Miller's cornfield. The fight surges back and forth across the rows, Confederate volleys cut down whole files, then Hood's Texans counter and slaughter Hooker's lead division in turn. Hooker is wounded. Mansfield is killed. The cornfield changes hands six times before stalemate.

annotations.text: Cornfield changes hands six times. ~8,000 casualties in three hours.

phases.title: Bloody Lane
phases.narration: Sumner's II Corps strikes the Confederate center along a sunken farm road. D.H. Hill's outnumbered division holds for hours from the natural trench. A misunderstood order swings a Confederate regiment perpendicular to the line and Union troops pour enfilading fire down its length. The Sunken Road becomes Bloody Lane.

annotations.text: Confederate center punctured but Sumner does not exploit. McClellan refuses to commit Porter's reserves.

phases.title: Burnside Bridge
phases.narration: On the Union left, Burnside spends three hours throwing brigades against a stone bridge held by 500 Georgians on the bluffs above. The creek is fordable in places but Burnside fixates on the bridge. When his men finally cross, Longstreet's thin line bends, and breaks open the road to Sharpsburg.

phases.title: A. P. Hill from Harpers Ferry
phases.narration: Burnside drives within sight of Sharpsburg. Lee's army is bent to the breaking point. Then A. P. Hill's Light Division, fifteen miles distant at dawn, arrives at a dead run from Harpers Ferry and slams into Burnside's exposed flank. The Union attack collapses. The sun sets on a tactical draw and the bloodiest day in American history.

units.label: A. P. Hill from the southwest

annotations.text: 22,717 American casualties in twelve hours. Lee withdraws across the Potomac the next night. Lincoln issues the Preliminary Emancipation Proclamation five days later.

normandy-1944.title: Normandy: The Longest Day
normandy-1944.intro: 6 June 1944. The Western Allies open the second front in Europe with the largest amphibious operation in history. 156,000 men land on five Norman beaches under cover of 6,939 vessels and 11,590 aircraft. By nightfall they hold a fragile coastal strip. Eleven months later the Reich Chancellery in Berlin will fly the red flag.
normandy-1944.battlefieldDesc: Eighty kilometers of Norman coast between the Cotentin Peninsula and the mouth of the Orne. Five sectors: Utah and Omaha for the Americans, Gold for the British 50th, Juno for the Canadians, Sword for the British 3rd. Behind them lies the bocage country, lethal for armor.

phases.title: Airborne
phases.narration: Three Allied airborne divisions drop into Normandy under a full moon. The American 82nd and 101st jump on the western flank around Sainte-Mère-Église, scattered by clouds and anti-aircraft fire across miles of bocage. The British 6th Airborne lands east of the Orne with one specific mission: seize the bridges at Bénouville and Ranville before the Germans can blow them.

phases.title: Pegasus Bridge
phases.narration: Major John Howard's company of the Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire Light Infantry rides six Horsa gliders down in the dark, the first one stopping 47 yards from the bridge over the Caen Canal. They take Pegasus Bridge and Horsa Bridge intact within ten minutes. The first liberated land in France is a French café on the canal bank, owned by Georges Gondrée.

phases.title: Pointe du Hoc
phases.narration: Lieutenant Colonel James Rudder's 2nd Ranger Battalion lands beneath a 30-meter cliff between Utah and Omaha. The Rangers fire grappling hooks, then climb under enemy grenades to silence a German battery the Allies had identified as a primary threat to the invasion fleet. They reach the top to find the guns gone, moved a kilometer inland. They find them anyway, in an apple orchard, and destroy them with thermite.

phases.title: The Fleet
phases.narration: Operation Neptune is the largest amphibious operation in history. 6,939 vessels carry 156,000 men across the Channel from southern England under cover of 11,590 aircraft. The naval bombardment opens at 05:30, with battleships including USS Texas, USS Arkansas, HMS Warspite, and HMS Ramillies firing at coastal batteries. The bombardment is too short and too far inland to destroy the bunkers on Omaha.

phases.title: Utah
phases.narration: The 4th Infantry Division lands a mile south of where its plan calls for, in a sector lightly defended by the 709th Static Division. Brigadier General Theodore Roosevelt Jr., Theodore's son, walks the beach with a cane and reports the error back: 'We'll start the war from right here.' The landing succeeds at the cost of fewer than 200 casualties on the beach itself.

phases.title: Omaha
phases.narration: The bloodiest beach. The 1st Infantry Division and the 29th Infantry Division come ashore beneath cliffs held by the 352nd Infantry Division, a full-strength field division the Allies had not identified. Of 32 DD tanks launched, 27 sink in the heavy seas. Landing craft drop their ramps into interlocking machine-gun fire from the bluffs. By noon the Americans hold a beach 100 yards deep at the cost of about 2,400 casualties.

phases.title: Gold, Juno, Sword
phases.narration: The British and Canadians come ashore an hour after the Americans, on a rising tide that pushes them past beach obstacles. The 50th Division takes Gold, including the harbor at Arromanches that will host the artificial Mulberry. The 3rd Canadian Division pushes inland fastest of anyone on D-Day, getting within 5 km of Caen. The British 3rd Division on Sword pushes toward Caen but stops short.

phases.title: 21st Panzer Counterattacks
phases.narration: 21st Panzer Division, the only armored formation in the immediate area, gets confused orders all day. By the time Feuchtinger drives north from Caen, the British 6th Airborne is dug in around Ranville and Allied air dominance is absolute. His tanks crest a ridge at Périers, see hundreds of gliders coming in to reinforce the British, and pull back. The opportunity for a decisive counterattack on D-Day is gone.

phases.title: Beaches Link Up
phases.narration: Bayeux falls intact on the morning of 7 June, the first French city liberated. Over the next week the five beach lodgements widen and meet. The Americans on Omaha link with the British on Gold at Port-en-Bessin on 8 June. The 101st and 4th Division clear Carentan on the 12th, joining Utah to Omaha. By the end of D+7 the Allied front is a continuous lodgement 80 km wide and 25 km deep.

phases.title: Cherbourg
phases.narration: VII Corps under Major General J. Lawton Collins drives north up the Cotentin Peninsula. Karl-Wilhelm von Schlieben holds Cherbourg with about 40,000 men, ordered by Hitler to fight to the last cartridge. The Americans take Cherbourg on the 26th. The port itself has been so thoroughly demolished by the Germans that it cannot be used at full capacity until September, but its capture confirms the Allies cannot be thrown back into the sea.

phases.title: The Lodgement Holds
phases.narration: By the end of June the Allies have 850,000 men, 150,000 vehicles, and 570,000 tons of supplies ashore. Two Mulberry harbors at Omaha and Arromanches replace the demolished Cherbourg until that port comes back online. Caen will hold for another month. But the strategic question, can the Allies stay, has been answered. The bocage fighting that follows will take through August. The breakout (Operation Cobra) opens on 25 July.

inchon-1950.title: Inchon: The Masterstroke
inchon-1950.intro: September 1950. The Korean People's Army has the UN forces pinned in the Pusan Perimeter at the southern tip of the peninsula. MacArthur stakes everything on an amphibious landing at Inchon, 240 kilometers behind enemy lines, in a harbor with 9-meter tides, sea walls, and a narrow channel. The Joint Chiefs call it reckless. He goes anyway.
inchon-1950.battlefieldDesc: Inchon harbor and approach. Wolmi-do (Moontip Island) at the harbor entrance, Red Beach against the city's sea wall to the north, Blue Beach on the southern flats. Seoul lies 30 km inland to the east.

phases.title: Wolmi-do, 6:30 a.m.
phases.narration: The narrow Flying Fish Channel forbids a one-stage assault: only the morning and evening high tides let landing craft cross the mud. The 5th Marines hit Wolmi-do at dawn, smother the guns that command the harbor mouth, and dig in. The fleet then withdraws to await the evening tide for the main landings.

phases.title: Red and Blue Beaches, 5:30 p.m.
phases.narration: With the harbor entrance held, the main landings come on the evening tide. 5th Marines scale Red Beach's sea wall with cargo ladders. 1st Marines hit Blue Beach to the south through mud and machine-gun fire. By midnight a full Marine regimental combat team is ashore and pushing into the city.

phases.title: Drive on Kimpo and the Han
phases.narration: X Corps consolidates ashore and drives inland. The 5th Marines seize Kimpo airfield on the 18th. Tactical air can now operate from Korean soil. The 7th Marines arrive and the 7th Infantry Division (Army) lands the second wave. On 20 September the Marines cross the Han River north of Seoul.

phases.title: Seoul retaken
phases.narration: Marines and Army units fight block by block through the South Korean capital against KPA holdouts. Behind them, the Eighth Army breaks out of Pusan to the south. KPA divisions, suddenly facing encirclement, dissolve. By the end of September South Korea is reclaimed and UN forces are at the 38th parallel.

annotations.text: MacArthur formally returns Seoul to Syngman Rhee on 29 September. KPA destroyed as a fighting force, until China crosses the Yalu six weeks later.

mogadishu-1993.title: Mogadishu: Black Hawk Down
mogadishu-1993.intro: 3 October 1993. Task Force Ranger launches a daylight raid into the heart of Mogadishu to capture two top lieutenants of warlord Mohamed Farrah Aidid. The hour-long operation spirals into fifteen hours of urban combat after two MH-60 Black Hawks are shot down. By dawn 18 Americans are dead and the policy of nation-building in Somalia is finished.
mogadishu-1993.battlefieldDesc: Bakara Market district, central Mogadishu. Olympic Hotel to the south, target building one block north, two crash sites in the densely-built urban grid.
mogadishu-1993.factionA: Task Force Ranger (US Army + Delta + 160th SOAR + UNOSOM relief column)

phases.title: The raid, 15:42
phases.narration: Ground convoy of Humvees and 5-ton trucks rolls south through Mogadishu. Above the target house, 19 Black Hawks and Little Birds insert Delta operators on the roof and four chalks of Rangers in blocking positions at the corners. Within minutes the prisoners are secured.

phases.title: Super Six-One down
phases.narration: As the convoy prepares to leave with the prisoners, an RPG strikes Black Hawk Super Six-One. The helicopter spirals into a tin-roofed alley five blocks northeast of the target. A search-and-rescue element fast-ropes in to the crash site. Minutes later Super Six-Four is hit and goes down a kilometer south.

annotations.text: Gordon and Shughart volunteer to defend Crash 2 alone. Both are killed. Both receive the Medal of Honor.

phases.title: The night perimeter
phases.narration: Cut off in the alleys around Crash 1, Rangers and Delta operators consolidate a defensive perimeter in houses overnight. Spectre gunships orbit overhead, called in on hand-held GPS, firing on militia massing in the streets. The convoy attempts twice to reach the crash site and is repulsed both times.

phases.title: Relief column at dawn
phases.narration: A composite column, UNOSOM Pakistani M-48s, Malaysian APCs, the US 10th Mountain Division, pushes through to Crash 1 at first light. The survivors withdraw under fire on foot for the last kilometer to the armor, the "Mogadishu Mile." 18 Americans are dead, 73 wounded, several hundred Somalis killed.

annotations.text: President Clinton orders US withdrawal from Somalia six months later.

verdun-1916.title: Verdun: They Shall Not Pass
