verdun-1916.intro: 21 February 1916. Falkenhayn launches Operation Gericht, a deliberate plan to "bleed France white" at a fortress city whose loss is politically intolerable. The longest battle of the war begins. By December the front has barely moved. Over 700,000 men are dead, wounded, or missing.
verdun-1916.battlefieldDesc: Verdun salient on the Meuse River. Fort Douaumont, Fort Vaux, and a ring of forts on the east bank. Mort-Homme and Côte 304 on the west bank. The Voie Sacrée, the only road south to Bar-le-Duc, is France's umbilical cord.

phases.title: Operation Gericht opens
phases.narration: Falkenhayn's nine-hour bombardment, 1,200 guns firing over a million shells in a single day, falls on a narrow eight-mile front. Storm troopers using flamethrowers and the first widespread use of phosgene gas advance into a moonscape. The French XXX Corps is shattered.

phases.title: Douaumont falls, without a fight
phases.narration: Fort Douaumont, France's strongest fortress, has been all but stripped of guns. A handful of German pioneers walk through an open postern and capture it without firing a shot. Pétain takes command of Second Army with the order: "Ils ne passeront pas." The Voie Sacrée begins moving 3,500 trucks a day.

annotations.text: 70% of all French infantry divisions rotate through Verdun. Pétain's noria keeps morale alive.

phases.title: Mort-Homme and Côte 304
phases.narration: Unable to crack the east bank quickly, the Germans extend the offensive to the west bank: Le Mort-Homme (Dead Man's Hill) and Côte 304. Both change hands repeatedly. June: Fort Vaux falls after a week of underground gas-and-flamethrower fighting. July: the Somme opens 200 km north, drawing German reserves away.

phases.title: Nivelle's counter-offensives
phases.narration: With German troops siphoned to the Somme, Nivelle plans a methodical retaking. A creeping barrage, rolled forward at 100 meters every four minutes, covers the assault. On 24 October Fort Douaumont is retaken. Vaux follows in November. By year's end the front sits roughly where it began in February.

annotations.text: 300 days. ~378,000 French casualties, ~337,000 German. The map looks the same. "Verdun" becomes a metonym for industrial slaughter.

el-alamein-1942.title: El Alamein: Lightfoot, Crumbling, Supercharge
el-alamein-1942.intro: October 1942. Erwin Rommel's Panzerarmee Afrika is stalled 100 km west of Alexandria after a 1,500 km advance across Libya and into Egypt. Bernard Montgomery has spent two months rebuilding the British 8th Army for one set-piece attack to break it. By the time the battle ends three weeks later, the Anglo-American Operation Torch has landed in Morocco and Algeria. The German position in North Africa is caught between two armies. Tunisia will fall in May 1943.
el-alamein-1942.battlefieldDesc: A 65 km gap between the Mediterranean coast in the north and the impassable Qattara Depression in the south. No flanks. The battle is a frontal grinding match across sand, ridges, and minefields.

phases.title: The Line at El Alamein
phases.narration: Erwin Rommel's Panzerarmee Afrika has been driven 1,500 km from Egypt the year before, only to come surging back across Libya after the spring of 1942. He is stopped 100 km short of Alexandria at a narrow corridor where the Mediterranean coast on the north and the impassable Qattara Depression on the south leave only a 65 km gap. Bernard Montgomery has spent two months building up the British 8th Army to break him. Rommel, sick, has flown to Austria to recover. General Georg Stumme commands in his place.

phases.title: Operation Lightfoot
phases.narration: The artillery preparation by nearly a thousand guns is the heaviest barrage the British have fired since the First World War. Four infantry divisions of XXX Corps advance behind the barrage on a four-mile front, clearing two corridors through 500,000 German and Italian mines, the 'Devil's Gardens.' Stumme dies of a heart attack on the first morning. The infantry phase clears most of the way to Miteirya Ridge but the armor cannot follow through the corridors fast enough.

phases.title: Crumbling
phases.narration: Montgomery's plan shifts to attrition. Rommel returns on the 25th and finds his army frozen in place. Each day Montgomery pushes a different brigade or two against the Italian and German line, drawing in the panzers piecemeal and grinding them down in armored exchanges around Kidney Ridge and Outpost Snipe. By the 28th the Italian Trieste and Bologna divisions are spent. Rommel has 81 tanks running against 800 British.

phases.title: Supercharge
phases.narration: Montgomery shifts his point of main effort south of the Australian sector and launches Operation Supercharge, a new infantry-and-armor breakthrough aimed at Tel el Aqqaqir. The 151st Brigade and 152nd Brigade fight through to the objective. The 9th Armoured Brigade sacrifices itself in a dawn charge that opens a corridor for the 1st Armoured Division. Rommel signals Berlin that the Panzerarmee can no longer hold. Hitler's stand-fast order arrives. Rommel obeys for one day, then begins the retreat on 4 November.

phases.title: The Long Retreat
phases.narration: Rommel withdraws along the coast road. Heavy rain breaks early and bogs down Montgomery's pursuit, allowing what is left of the Panzerarmee to escape with most of its German units intact, though the Italian infantry divisions are lost. Tobruk falls on 13 November, Benghazi on the 20th. Three days after Alamein opens the Allies land in Morocco and Algeria (Operation Torch). The whole German position in North Africa is now caught between two armies. It will surrender in Tunisia in May 1943, with 275,000 Axis soldiers captured.

vicksburg-1863.title: Vicksburg: The Mississippi Cut
vicksburg-1863.intro: Spring 1863. Vicksburg sits on bluffs commanding a hairpin bend of the Mississippi, the last Confederate stronghold on the river. Lincoln calls it "the key." After eighteen months of failed approaches, Grant cuts loose from his supply line, marches inland, and beats two Confederate armies in five battles in eighteen days.
vicksburg-1863.battlefieldDesc: Mississippi River bends west around Vicksburg's bluffs. Big Black River flows southwest into it. Five battlefields between Bruinsburg landing and the city: Port Gibson, Raymond, Jackson, Champion Hill, Big Black River Bridge.

phases.title: The crossing at Bruinsburg
phases.narration: Porter's gunboats run the Vicksburg batteries at night. Grant marches his army down the west bank of the Mississippi and ferries it across at Bruinsburg, well below the city. Pemberton's Confederate garrison is fixed in place by feints from Sherman north of the city. Grant deliberately abandons his supply line: the army will live off the country.

phases.title: Port Gibson and Raymond
phases.narration: McClernand defeats a Confederate brigade at Port Gibson on 1 May. McPherson takes Raymond on the 12th. Grant pushes inland, north toward Vicksburg or east toward Jackson? He chooses east first: take out Joe Johnston's relief force before turning on Pemberton.

phases.title: Jackson and Champion Hill
phases.narration: Grant takes Jackson on 14 May, scattering Johnston's force, then pivots west. On 16 May Pemberton, under contradictory orders from Davis (hold Vicksburg) and Johnston (link up east), meets Grant on the Champion Hill plateau. After day-long fighting, McPherson's flanking maneuver shatters Pemberton's line. The Confederates fall back to the Big Black River.

phases.title: Investment and the siege
phases.narration: Pemberton's army falls back into Vicksburg's fortifications. Grant's two frontal assaults on 19 and 22 May are repulsed at heavy cost. He settles into a siege. For 47 days the city is shelled day and night. Civilians live in hillside caves. Rations dwindle to mule meat. On 4 July, the day after Pickett's Charge, Pemberton surrenders 29,495 men. Five days later Port Hudson falls. The Mississippi runs unvexed.

annotations.text: 29,495 Confederates surrender. The Mississippi is Union from Cairo to the Gulf. The Confederacy is split.

battle-of-britain-1940.title: Battle of Britain: The Few
battle-of-britain-1940.intro: July–October 1940. With France fallen, only Britain stands. Hitler needs air superiority before an invasion fleet can cross the Channel. Göring promises it in four weeks. The Luftwaffe outnumbers RAF Fighter Command 2:1, but radar, the Dowding system, and pilots fighting over home ground tilt the math.
battle-of-britain-1940.battlefieldDesc: Southern England and the Channel. Fighter Command's Group sectors visible at the airfields. Luftwaffe bases line the French and Low Countries coast.

phases.title: Kanalkampf, the Channel battle
phases.narration: Luftwaffe attacks Channel convoys and coastal radar stations to lure RAF fighters into combat over water, where downed British pilots are lost. Dowding husbands his squadrons. Radar guides them in only when needed. The trade is uneven but the system works.

phases.title: Adlerangriff, Eagle Day and after
phases.narration: Göring shifts to a knockout campaign against Fighter Command's airfields and sector stations. RAF loss rates exceed replacement. Pilots fly four or five sorties a day. By early September 11 Group's southern sector stations are visibly degrading. The campaign is on the verge of working.

annotations.text: Fighter Command pilot losses exceed training output for six straight weeks.

phases.title: The switch to London
phases.narration: After a stray Luftwaffe bomb hits London and Bomber Command retaliates against Berlin, Hitler orders the Luftwaffe to switch from airfields to terror-bombing London. The blow saves Fighter Command at the moment it is most exhausted. RAF squadrons rebuild in the relative quiet of the Sector stations.

phases.title: 15 September, The Hardest Day
phases.narration: Two massed Luftwaffe raids on London meet a fully prepared Fighter Command. Every 11 Group squadron is up. 12 Group's Big Wing intercepts the second wave. The Luftwaffe loses 60 aircraft for 28 RAF. Two days later Hitler postpones Operation Sea Lion indefinitely.

annotations.text: Churchill: "Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few."

iwo-jima-1945.title: Iwo Jima: Suribachi and the Meatgrinder
iwo-jima-1945.intro: 19 February 1945. Three Marine divisions land on an eight-square-mile volcanic island halfway between Saipan and Tokyo. They need it for the air bases that will let B-29s reach Japan with fighter escort. Kuribayashi's 21,000 defenders, dug into a honeycomb of tunnels and pillboxes, mean to bleed every yard.
iwo-jima-1945.battlefieldDesc: Pork-chop-shaped volcanic island. Mount Suribachi (165m) at the southwest tip. Airfields in the center. Broken hills of the Motoyama plateau in the north, the Meatgrinder.

phases.title: D-Day landings
phases.narration: After three days of naval bombardment, the 4th and 5th Marine Divisions land on the southeast beaches. The volcanic ash is so soft that tracked vehicles bog down. Kuribayashi holds his fire until the beaches are crowded, then opens up from Suribachi and from the high ground inland. By nightfall the Marines hold a strip of ash 800 meters deep.

phases.title: Suribachi, the flag
phases.narration: The 28th Marines cut Suribachi off from the rest of the island on day two and spend four days reducing its pillboxes one by one with grenades, flamethrowers, and demolition charges. On 23 February a patrol reaches the summit and raises a small flag. A few hours later a larger flag goes up, Joe Rosenthal's photograph.

annotations.text: Three of the six flag-raisers will die before Iwo Jima is secured.

phases.title: The Meatgrinder, Motoyama
phases.narration: North of Airfield No. 1, the ground rises into broken volcanic terrain, the Motoyama plateau. Kuribayashi's main defensive belt runs across it. The Marines name the worst sectors: Charlie-Dog Ridge, Turkey Knob, the Amphitheater. Progress is measured in yards. The 3rd Marine Division lands and is fed in beside the 4th and 5th.

phases.title: Kitano Point and the end
phases.narration: Kuribayashi's command is pushed back into a final pocket at Kitano Point on the northwest tip. He radios his last message on 17 March. Organized resistance ends on 26 March with a final banzai charge through the rear-area camps. Iwo Jima costs 6,800 American dead, and the island's airfields save the lives of thousands of B-29 crews in the months that follow.

annotations.text: Of 21,000 defenders, ~216 are captured alive. The first B-29 emergency landing at Iwo Jima occurs on 4 March, with the battle still raging.

yorktown-1781.title: Yorktown: The Last Siege
yorktown-1781.intro: September 1781. Cornwallis encamps his army at Yorktown to await Royal Navy resupply. Washington and Rochambeau, learning a French fleet under de Grasse is steaming north, march 700 kilometers in five weeks to trap him. When the British relief fleet arrives, de Grasse has already won the Chesapeake. Cornwallis is alone.
yorktown-1781.battlefieldDesc: Yorktown peninsula on the York River. British inner works ring the town. Outer redoubts (No. 9 and No. 10) anchor the southeast corner. Franco-American siege lines invest from the south.

phases.title: The Chesapeake closed
phases.narration: Admiral de Grasse leaves the West Indies in August with 28 ships of the line and lands 3,200 French troops at the head of the Chesapeake. On 5 September his fleet drives off Admiral Graves's British squadron at the Battle of the Virginia Capes. The Royal Navy will not return to Cornwallis's relief.

phases.title: Investment
phases.narration: Washington's army arrives from New York joined by Rochambeau's French regulars. 17,600 allied troops invest 8,300 British. The first parallel, a siege trench 600 meters from the British works, is opened on the night of 6 October. French and Continental artillery is dragged into position.

phases.title: Redoubts 9 and 10
phases.narration: The second parallel cannot be completed without taking the outer redoubts. Two assaults go in at night with unloaded muskets: French grenadiers against No. 9, Alexander Hamilton's Continental light infantry against No. 10. Both are taken in under fifteen minutes. The second parallel is finished and Continental guns can fire directly into the British works at close range.

phases.title: Parley and surrender
phases.narration: Cornwallis attempts a sortie on the night of the 15th, then a desperate plan to escape across the York River to Gloucester Point and break out overland. A squall scatters the boats. On 17 October a drummer boy beats out a parley signal. Two days later 7,087 British and Hessian soldiers march out and lay down their arms while the band plays "The World Turned Upside Down."

annotations.text: When the news reaches London in late November, Lord North reportedly cries: "Oh God! It is all over!"

khe-sanh-1968.title: Khe Sanh: The Hill Country Siege
khe-sanh-1968.intro: January 1968. Two divisions of the People's Army of Vietnam encircle the US Marine combat base at Khe Sanh near the Laotian border. President Johnson keeps a sand-table replica in the White House Situation Room. Westmoreland sees a chance at a decisive battle on American terms. For 77 days the Marines and air power hold.
khe-sanh-1968.battlefieldDesc: Khe Sanh plateau in northwest South Vietnam, ringed by jungle-covered hills 881, 861, and 558 north and west. Route 9 east toward Da Nang. Airstrip in the center of the base.

phases.title: Encirclement
phases.narration: PAVN sappers strike Hill 861 and demolish the main ammunition dump on the base. By dawn the base is invested. The 26th Marines hold strongpoints on Hills 881 South, 861, 558, and 950, with the main base in the bowl below.

phases.title: Operation Niagara
phases.narration: Westmoreland orders a tactical air campaign of unprecedented scale: B-52 arc-light strikes within hundreds of meters of Marine perimeters. A-6s and Marine A-4s in close support. C-130s with low-altitude LAPES extractions to keep the base supplied when the airstrip is under fire. PAVN trenches creep ever closer to the perimeter.

annotations.text: Niagara drops more than 100,000 tons of bombs in 77 days, more than on the entire Pacific War in 1942–43.

phases.title: Hill battles and the Tet diversion
phases.narration: While Khe Sanh holds attention, the Tet Offensive erupts across South Vietnam. PAVN attacks on the hill positions intensify: Hill 64 (a Lang Vei special-forces camp 8 km west) is overrun by Soviet PT-76 tanks. The hill outposts of 861A, 881S, and 558 repel mass assaults.

phases.title: Operation Pegasus, the relief
phases.narration: 1st Cavalry Division (Airmobile) leapfrogs companies by Huey down Route 9 from the east, reopening the road. The siege is declared lifted on 8 April. Within months Westmoreland's replacement, Creighton Abrams, orders Khe Sanh abandoned and stripped, the bunkers blown, the runway broken up. The two sides argue for decades over who won.

annotations.text: ~205 US dead at Khe Sanh. PAVN losses estimated 10,000–15,000. Days later the base is bulldozed.

bunker-hill-1775.title: Bunker Hill: The Costly Lesson
bunker-hill-1775.intro: 17 June 1775. Two months after Lexington and Concord, colonial militia entrench overnight on Breed's Hill, a closer eminence to Boston than the named hill, to threaten the British garrison. General Gage decides to clear them with a frontal assault by infantry in line. The lesson is paid for in three waves up the slope.
bunker-hill-1775.battlefieldDesc: Charlestown peninsula, north shore of Boston Harbor. Breed's Hill overlooks the British fleet anchored in the harbor. Bunker Hill rises behind. Mystic River to the north, Charles River to the south.

phases.title: The redoubt on Breed's Hill
phases.narration: Colonel William Prescott's 1,200 militiamen, ordered to fortify Bunker Hill, instead dig in on Breed's Hill, closer to the harbor and within range of the British fleet. By dawn a square earthwork redoubt 8 feet high stands on the hill. A rail fence and stone wall extend the line northeast to the Mystic River shore.

phases.title: The first assault
phases.narration: General William Howe advances 2,200 regulars in line up Breed's Hill in two columns. Prescott orders his men to hold fire "until you see the whites of their eyes", until 30 paces. The volley shatters the British formation. Whole files go down. The column withdraws to dress ranks at the base of the hill.

phases.title: The second assault
phases.narration: Howe reorganizes, draws fresh troops, and tries the same approach, this time with HMS Somerset shelling the redoubt and a separate column attacking the rail fence. Both attacks fail again under disciplined militia volleys. Charlestown is set ablaze by red-hot shot from the fleet to deny it as cover. British losses are now severe.

phases.title: The third assault, bayonet over the wall
phases.narration: Howe strips his men of packs and orders a third attack against the redoubt alone, with bayonets only, no firing on the advance. Militia powder runs out as the column nears the parapet. The British come over the wall. Prescott's men fall back through Bunker Hill behind, abandoning the field. Casualties: 226 militia killed, 305 British killed, 828 British wounded. Gage writes home that another such victory would ruin the army.

annotations.text: Gen. Gage: "The trials we have had show that the rebels are not the despicable rabble too many have supposed them to be."

bulge-1944.title: Battle of the Bulge: Watch on the Rhine
bulge-1944.intro: 16 December 1944. Hitler launches his last strategic offensive in the West. Three German armies attack on a 65-mile front through the Ardennes Forest, aimed at the port of Antwerp. The American line is held by four thin, underestimated divisions. Six weeks later, after 81,000 American casualties and 100,000 German, the bulge is pinched off and the panzer reserve held for the Eastern Front is gone.
bulge-1944.battlefieldDesc: Forested hill country of eastern Belgium and Luxembourg. Roads run east to west through narrow valleys. The Ardennes is poor tank terrain, which is exactly why the Allies thought it could be lightly held.

phases.title: Watch on the Rhine
phases.narration: Hitler launches his last strategic offensive in the West. Three German armies, the 6th SS Panzer Army under Sepp Dietrich, the 5th Panzer Army under Hasso von Manteuffel, and the 7th Army under Erich Brandenberger, attack on a 65-mile front through the Ardennes Forest. Their objective is the port of Antwerp. The American line is held by four thinly stretched divisions, two of them green and two recovering from the Hürtgen Forest. Fog grounds Allied tactical air for the first six days.

phases.title: Peiper's Spearhead
phases.narration: Joachim Peiper's Kampfgruppe of 1st SS Panzer Division leads the northern thrust. His tanks reach Stavelot before dawn on the 18th and shoot up an American fuel dump. American POWs of the 285th Field Artillery Observation Battalion are machine-gunned at Malmedy on the 17th, 84 dead. Peiper captures La Gleize and pushes for the Meuse. He runs out of fuel at Stoumont and is checked there by the 30th Infantry Division. By the 24th his survivors abandon their vehicles and walk out on foot.

phases.title: Elsenborn Holds
phases.narration: The American 99th and 2nd Infantry Divisions on Elsenborn Ridge refuse to break. Dietrich's panzers cannot get off the Losheim road network. The high ground on the northern shoulder, called the Eisenhower line afterward, holds for the entire battle. This forces every subsequent German thrust to angle southwest, the wrong direction for the Antwerp objective, and confines the offensive to a narrow tongue between Elsenborn and Bastogne.

phases.title: Saint-Vith Falls
phases.narration: Manteuffel's 5th Panzer Army overruns the 106th Infantry Division in the Schnee Eifel, with two regiments forced to surrender, the largest American capitulation of the European war. Bruce Clarke's Combat Command B of the 7th Armored Division holds Saint-Vith for six days under increasing pressure, finally yielding the town on the 21st. The fight delays the German timetable badly. Without Saint-Vith on schedule the offensive cannot reach the Meuse.

phases.title: Bastogne
phases.narration: Bastogne is a seven-road junction in the central Ardennes and a German priority. McAuliffe's 101st Airborne reaches the town on the 19th, ahead of the Germans, with elements of the 10th Armored Division. The Germans cut the roads on the 20th. McAuliffe is asked to surrender on the 22nd and replies 'Nuts!' Bad weather lifts on the 23rd, and Allied tactical air finally arrives. Patton's 4th Armored Division of III Corps reaches Bastogne from the south on the afternoon of the 26th, after a 100-mile pivot in 48 hours.

phases.title: The Meuse
phases.narration: 2nd Panzer Division reaches Celles, four miles from the Meuse at Dinant, on Christmas Eve. They have run on fumes for two days. British 29th Armoured Brigade tanks watch from the west bank of the river. American 2nd Armored Division, brought down from the Aachen front, attacks from the north on Christmas Day. By the 26th the German spearhead is destroyed in the Celles pocket. The Meuse is never crossed. The deepest point of the bulge.

phases.title: Closing the Bulge
phases.narration: Patton attacks from the south and Hodges from the north, meeting at Houffalize on the 16th of January. The bulge is pinched off. The original front line is restored by the 25th. German losses are roughly 100,000, including the best of the panzer reserve held for a counterattack on the Eastern Front. American losses are about 81,000, with 19,000 dead. The strategic effect is to bring the Eastern Front offensive opening week earlier, since the Wehrmacht has nothing left to oppose Zhukov.

kursk-1943.title: Kursk: The Largest Tank Battle
kursk-1943.intro: July 1943. The Kursk salient bulges 150 kilometers into German lines. Hitler delays his offensive (Citadel) for new Panther and Tiger tanks. The Soviets use the months to dig eight defensive belts, lay 503,000 mines, and assemble 1.3 million troops in depth. When Citadel finally opens, it strikes the deepest defensive system in history.
kursk-1943.battlefieldDesc: Kursk salient: Orel to the north, Belgorod to the south, Kursk city in the center. German pincers strike from north (9th Army) and south (4th Panzer Army + Army Detachment Kempf) to bite off the salient.

phases.title: Citadel opens
phases.narration: Citadel begins with both German pincers attacking on the same day. In the north Model's 9th Army grinds slowly into Rokossovsky's defenses, advancing only 6–8 km in three days. In the south Manstein achieves more, Hoth's 4th Panzer Army penetrates 30 km, but every meter is paid for in Tigers and Panthers. The Soviet defense in depth is doing its job.

annotations.text: 503,000 Soviet mines. 8 defensive belts to 250 km depth.

phases.title: Northern pincer stalls
phases.narration: Model commits his armor too early into broken ground. The 9th Army takes the Olkhovatka heights but stops cold against the second defensive belt at Ponyri. After five days Model's spearheads have advanced 14 km against orders to reach 100 km. On 12 July Rokossovsky launches the Operation Kutuzov counter-offensive that turns the German salient at Orel into Model's problem.

phases.title: Prokhorovka
phases.narration: Manstein's southern thrust drives toward the rail junction at Prokhorovka. Vatutin commits Rotmistrov's 5th Guards Tank Army in a head-on charge to keep the SS panzer corps off balance. Hundreds of tanks meet in confused close-range fighting on the Psel steppe. Soviet losses are severe but the German exploitation force is exhausted. Hitler, hearing of the Allied landings in Sicily that morning, halts Citadel.

annotations.text: 12 July also: Allies land in Sicily. Hitler suspends Citadel two days later.

phases.title: The Soviet rolling offensive
phases.narration: Three Soviet operations follow: Kutuzov rolls up the Orel salient in the north. Rumyantsev liberates Belgorod and Kharkov in the south. The Donbass operation widens the front. Citadel has cost the Wehrmacht its eastern reserve. After Kursk the Red Army is on the offensive for the rest of the war.

coral-sea-1942.title: Coral Sea: The First Carrier Duel
coral-sea-1942.intro: May 1942. Japan moves to seize Port Moresby on Papua and isolate Australia. Two opposing carrier task forces, neither of which ever sights the other's ships, search for each other across the Coral Sea. For the first time in history a fleet battle is fought entirely by aircraft from carriers.
coral-sea-1942.battlefieldDesc: Coral Sea between New Guinea (top), the Solomons (right), and northeast Australia (bottom). Tulagi at top right. Port Moresby at top left. The carrier groups maneuver in the open sea between.

phases.title: MO Operation and the Allied trap
phases.narration: Operation MO sends two Japanese forces south: an invasion convoy bound for Port Moresby, escorted by light carrier Shōhō, and a striking force built around fleet carriers Shōkaku and Zuikaku, looping east of the Solomons to ambush any Allied response. Nimitz, reading the JN-25 code, has Fletcher's TF 17 (Yorktown + Lexington) waiting in the Coral Sea.

phases.title: "Scratch one flattop"
phases.narration: Both sides launch strikes at false sightings, Japanese aircraft sink the oiler Neosho and destroyer Sims. American aircraft find and sink the light carrier Shōhō in ten minutes ("Scratch one flattop," Dixon's famous radio call). The Moresby invasion convoy turns back, never to land. The big carriers still circle each other in the dark.

annotations.text: Bob Dixon: "Scratch one flattop! Dixon to carrier, scratch one flattop!"

phases.title: Carriers find carriers
phases.narration: At dawn each side finds the other. Both launch full strikes simultaneously. Japanese pilots score torpedo and bomb hits on Lexington and Yorktown. American pilots heavily damage Shōkaku and savage Zuikaku's air group. By afternoon all four fleet carriers are out of action, but Lexington's ruptured aviation gasoline lines spark fires that doom her. She is scuttled at sunset.

phases.title: Verdict, and what Midway will mean
phases.narration: Tactically Japan trades a light carrier and an air group for a fleet carrier sunk and another damaged, a tactical Japanese win on tonnage. Strategically the Allies win: Moresby is not invaded, and both Shōkaku and Zuikaku are unavailable for the Midway operation a month later. The IJN has six fleet carriers. At Midway it brings four. Coral Sea takes two off the board.

annotations.text: Yorktown returns to Pearl Harbor on 27 May. Emergency repairs are completed in 72 hours. She sorties for Midway 30 May.

okinawa-1945.title: Okinawa: The Typhoon of Steel
okinawa-1945.intro: 1 April 1945, Easter Sunday and April Fool's Day. The Tenth Army lands on Okinawa, the last major Pacific island before the Japanese home islands, in the largest amphibious operation of the Pacific War. 183,000 Marines and soldiers come ashore against 100,000 dug-in defenders. The 82-day battle costs more American lives than any other in the Pacific.
okinawa-1945.battlefieldDesc: Okinawa, 110 km long, oriented roughly NE-SW. Hagushi beaches (west), Yontan and Kadena airfields (center). Northern jungle peninsula (Motobu) light. Southern Shuri massif heavily fortified.

phases.title: Unopposed landing
phases.narration: Buckner's Tenth Army, III Amphibious Corps (Marines) and XXIV Corps (Army), lands on the Hagushi beaches against almost no resistance. Yontan and Kadena airfields fall the first day. Ushijima has deliberately ceded the beaches: he plans to bleed the Americans against fortifications on the Shuri Line in the south.

phases.title: Kamikaze and the picket line
phases.narration: Operation Ten-Go unleashes the largest organized kamikaze campaign of the war, ten mass attacks (Kikusui) over twelve weeks. Radar pickets ringing the island take the brunt: 36 ships sunk, 368 damaged, ~5,000 sailors killed. The super-battleship Yamato is sent on a one-way sortie on 7 April and is sunk by US carrier aircraft before it reaches the island.

annotations.text: 36 US ships sunk and 368 damaged at sea. ~4,900 US Navy dead, more than the ground forces' KIA combined.

phases.title: Shuri Line and Sugar Loaf
phases.narration: XXIV Corps grinds south against the Shuri Line, a series of mutually supporting ridges defended by entrenched infantry and artillery. The 6th Marine Division pays for Sugar Loaf Hill seven times before they hold it. Buckner is killed on 18 June by Japanese artillery. The highest-ranking American officer to die from enemy fire in WWII. Ushijima commits ritual suicide on 22 June.

phases.title: The end of the campaign
phases.narration: Organized resistance ends on 22 June. 92,000 Japanese soldiers and ~150,000 Okinawan civilians die in the battle. American losses exceed 49,000 including 12,500 killed. Planners in Washington study the casualty figures and project a million American casualties for the invasion of Japan. Six weeks later the atomic bombs fall on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

annotations.text: Okinawa's bloodletting weighs on Truman's decision on the atomic bomb. Operation Olympic, set for 1 November, never happens.

chosin-reservoir-1950.title: Chosin Reservoir: Frozen Chosin
chosin-reservoir-1950.intro: November 1950. After Inchon and the recapture of Seoul, MacArthur's army drives north toward the Yalu. The 1st Marine Division advances up a single mountain road to the Chosin Reservoir at the roof of Korea. Unseen, twelve PVA divisions of Song Shilun's 9th Army Group encircle them in temperatures of −37 °C.
chosin-reservoir-1950.battlefieldDesc: Chosin Reservoir, high mountain plateau. Yudam-ni on the west side of the reservoir. Hagaru-ri at the southern tip. Koto-ri and Hungnam further down the only road south through Funchilin Pass.

phases.title: The drive to the Yalu
phases.narration: 1st Marine Division and elements of 7th Infantry Division have advanced 80 kilometers up the only road from Hungnam to the reservoir, halting at Yudam-ni on the west side and Hagaru-ri at the south. Smith, the Marine division commander, has insisted on building an airstrip at Hagaru-ri against Almond's orders, a decision that will save the division. The temperature drops to −37 °C.

phases.title: Ambush
phases.narration: After dark on 27 November the PVA strikes simultaneously: Yudam-ni and Hagaru-ri perimeters are hit by mass infantry assaults. RCT-31 east of the reservoir ("Task Force Faith") is overrun in pieces and ceases to exist as a fighting force. Fox Company, 7th Marines holds Toktong Pass, the chokepoint of the only road back, with 246 men against successive battalion-scale attacks.

phases.title: "Attacking in a different direction"
phases.narration: The Yudam-ni regiments fight 23 km back to Hagaru-ri along the road in temperatures that disable machine guns and freeze morphine syrettes. They reach the perimeter on 4 December bringing their wounded and most of their equipment. Air resupply by C-47s onto Smith's airstrip, which Marines have widened and lengthened under fire, keeps the column going. Smith to reporters: "Retreat hell! We're just attacking in a different direction."

phases.title: Funchilin Pass to the sea
phases.narration: Below Koto-ri the road crosses Funchilin Pass on a single bridge over a power-station penstock, which the PVA blow in three places. C-119 Boxcars airdrop eight 1,000-kg Treadway bridge sections. Combat engineers reassemble two of them across the gap under fire. The division crosses on 9 December, files down to Hungnam, and is evacuated by sea. Of the original 25,000, 7,400 are casualties. Only 198 are taken prisoner.

annotations.text: 9th Army Group is rendered combat-ineffective by Chosin and frostbite. Smith's division is the only major UN unit to fight intact to the coast.

berlin-1945.title: Berlin: The Reich Capital Falls
berlin-1945.intro: 16 April 1945. Three Soviet fronts, Zhukov in the center, Konev in the south, Rokossovsky on the right, open the final offensive of the European war. 2.3 million Red Army soldiers, 6,250 tanks, and 7,500 aircraft converge on a city whose defenders include Hitler Youth, Volkssturm pensioners, and the wreckage of formations that have been retreating for two years. In sixteen days the Reich Chancellery flies the red flag.
berlin-1945.battlefieldDesc: Eastern Germany. The Oder–Neisse line runs north–south, with Berlin 60 km behind it. Zhukov's 1st Belorussian attacks from the Seelow Heights, Konev's 1st Ukrainian wheels north from the Neisse, and the encirclement closes at Ketzin west of the city on 25 April.

phases.title: Dawn at the Seelow Heights
phases.narration: Zhukov opens with 9,000 guns and 143 anti-aircraft searchlights aimed at the German line, meant to blind the defenders. It backfires: Heinrici had pulled his frontline troops back overnight, so the barrage falls on empty trenches. The searchlights silhouette the advancing Soviet infantry against the dust. The 8th Guards Army wades into the Oderbruch lowlands and stalls under fire from the Heights above.

phases.title: The Heights Crack
phases.narration: Three days of grinding assault. Soviet armor is committed early, against doctrine, to force the breakthrough. 1st Guards Tank Army and 2nd Guards Tank Army push up the slopes under direct anti-tank fire. By the morning of the 19th the Seelow position is gone and the road to Berlin is open. The cost: 30,000 Soviet casualties and 743 tanks for a piece of ground 80 km from the capital.

phases.title: Konev's Southern Wheel
phases.narration: While Zhukov bleeds at Seelow, Konev's 1st Ukrainian Front breaks across the Neisse at Forst and Triebel. Schörner's 4th Panzer Army scatters. Konev senses opportunity and wheels his tank armies, the 3rd and 4th Guards Tank, northwest, not west, aimed directly at Berlin's southern districts. Stalin lets the race run between his two marshals.

phases.title: Encirclement Closes at Ketzin
phases.narration: Konev's 4th Guards Tank Army and Zhukov's 47th Army meet at Ketzin, west of Berlin. The ring is closed. Inside it: the entire 9th Army trapped in the Halbe pocket south of the city, the LVI Panzer Corps fallen back into the city, and the remnants of every formation Heinrici threw into the path. Outside it: the road to the Elbe is open and the Reich is about to be split.

phases.title: Handshake at Torgau
phases.narration: Sixty kilometers west of Berlin, on the wreckage of the Elbe bridge at Torgau, Lieutenant Kotzebue of the US 69th Infantry Division meets Lieutenant Silvashko of the Soviet 58th Guards Rifle Division. The Reich is cut in half. North and south of Torgau the front goes quiet within hours: the question of who reaches Berlin first has already been decided in Zhukov's favor.

phases.title: Eight Armies into the Suburbs
phases.narration: Eight Soviet armies enter Berlin from every direction at once: 47th and 3rd Shock from the north, 5th Shock and 8th Guards from the east, 1st Guards Tank from the southeast, 3rd Guards Tank and 8th Mechanized from the south, 28th Army from the southwest. Inside the city the defenders are a patchwork: LVI Panzer Corps, Waffen-SS Nordland, Volkssturm pensioners, and 15-year-olds of the Hitler Youth.

phases.title: Tempelhof
phases.narration: Chuikov's 8th Guards Army, the men who held Stalingrad, fight block by block up Tempelhofer Damm. The airfield itself, the Luftwaffe's lifeline into the city, falls late on the 26th. With Tempelhof gone the city can no longer be resupplied or evacuated by air. The last flight out carries General Ritter von Greim and Hanna Reitsch.

phases.title: Spree Crossings
phases.narration: The Spree cuts the city diagonally and the bridges are the last natural defense. Soviet engineers force the river under direct fire at the Moltke Bridge and the Hohenzollern Bridge, taking appalling casualties to win a meter of concrete at a time. By nightfall on the 29th, the Reichstag is one assault away, and all the politburo wants to know is whose flag will fly first.

phases.title: The Reichstag
phases.narration: Three battalions of the 150th Rifle Division, Neustroyev, Davydov, Samsonov, assault the Reichstag across 200 meters of open ground swept by machine-gun fire. Inside, ~1,000 SS and Volkssturm fight floor by floor with grenades and bayonets. By evening the Soviets are in the second story. Fighting continues through the night.

phases.title: Banner on the Dome
phases.narration: At 22:50 on 30 April, Sergeants Yegorov and Kantaria of the 756th Rifle Regiment force their way to the roof and tie the Banner of Victory, Soviet Military Council Banner No. 5, to a bronze equestrian statue on the western pediment. The photograph staged two days later is the one the world remembers. The actual flag raising happens in darkness, under fire.

phases.title: Inside the Bunker
phases.narration: Eight meters beneath the Reich Chancellery garden, Hitler shoots himself in the Führerbunker. Goebbels poisons his six children and follows on the 1st. The succession passes by codicil to Grand Admiral Karl Dönitz in Flensburg. The bunker's last radio message goes out to Dönitz at 15:18 on 1 May. The thousand-year Reich has 47 hours left.

phases.title: Karlshorst
phases.narration: General Weidling, the Berlin commandant, surrenders the garrison at six in the morning of 2 May. ~92,000 German soldiers are dead in the battle for the city. ~480,000 captured. ~81,000 Soviet soldiers killed, ~280,000 wounded across the full Strategic Offensive. Six days later, in Zhukov's headquarters in Karlshorst in the eastern suburbs, Field Marshal Keitel signs the unconditional surrender of all German armed forces. The European war is over.

somme-1916.title: The Somme: A Storm of Steel
somme-1916.intro: 1 July 1916. After a week of preparatory bombardment, eighteen British and French divisions go over the top along a 30-kilometer front in Picardy. Haig expects a breakthrough. He gets the worst day in British military history. The campaign drags into November, costs over a million casualties on both sides, and barely moves the line.
somme-1916.battlefieldDesc: Picardy chalk plateau. River Somme runs west. British line in the north against Thiepval, Beaumont-Hamel, La Boisselle. French line in the south against Maricourt and the Frise salient.

phases.title: The week-long bombardment
phases.narration: 1,500 British guns fire 1.6 million shells in the seven days before the assault, the largest preparation in the war so far. Plans assume the wire will be cut and German trenches will be unhabitable when the infantry steps off. Both assumptions are false: a third of British shells are duds, the wire stands in many sectors, and the Germans wait in 12-meter-deep dugouts.

phases.title: 1 July, the worst day
phases.narration: Whistles blow at 07:30. British infantry climb out of trenches and walk forward in ordered lines through gaps in their own wire. German machine gunners emerge from dugouts as the barrage lifts, set up, and open fire. By nightfall the British Army has 57,470 casualties, 19,240 killed, for almost no ground. The French in the south, attacking with creeping barrages and surprise, take their objectives.

annotations.text: 57,470 British casualties, single bloodiest day in British military history.

phases.title: Bite-and-hold
phases.narration: Haig switches to limited objective attacks behind creeping barrages. High Wood, Delville Wood, Pozières, each ridge is taken in costly local fighting. The 1st Australian Division loses 23,000 in seven weeks at Pozières. On 15 September Haig debuts tanks at Flers-Courcelette. 32 of 49 reach the start line, three reach the second German trench.

phases.title: Mud and the end
phases.narration: Autumn rain turns the battlefield into liquid chalk. The final phase, Beaumont-Hamel and Ancre, gains a few kilometers in the north. Haig calls off the offensive on 18 November. Total casualties: ~419,000 British, ~204,000 French, ~465,000 German. The line has moved 10 kilometers. The British have, however, bled the Imperial German Army's pre-war professionals beyond replacement.

annotations.text: Erich von Falkenhayn: "The Somme bled the German army white as Verdun did the French."

gallipoli-1915.title: Gallipoli: The Lost Gamble
gallipoli-1915.intro: April 1915. The British and French open a second front against the Ottoman Empire by landing on the Gallipoli peninsula, hoping to force the Dardanelles, take Constantinople, and reopen the supply route to Russia. The campaign was Churchill's idea. Eight months later the Allies have evacuated, having lost about 56,000 dead. The Ottoman defenders, commanded operationally by a 34-year-old colonel named Mustafa Kemal, have lost about 87,000 dead.
gallipoli-1915.battlefieldDesc: The narrow peninsula of European Turkey separating the Aegean from the Sea of Marmara. Steep cliffs at the landing beaches give the high ground to whoever holds the inland ridges, Sari Bair and Tekke Tepe.

phases.title: The Plan
phases.narration: First Lord of the Admiralty Winston Churchill argues that the war can be shortened by forcing the Dardanelles, knocking the Ottoman Empire out of the war, and reopening the supply route to Russia. The Royal Navy attempts a purely naval forcing on 18 March 1915. Three battleships are sunk by mines and the fleet pulls back. The Allies decide on a land campaign to clear the Turkish forts. Mustafa Kemal Bey, a 34-year-old Ottoman colonel, is deployed to the peninsula with the 19th Division.

phases.title: Landings at Helles
phases.narration: The 29th British Division lands at five small beaches at the tip of the peninsula. V Beach, in front of the village of Sedd el Bahr, becomes a slaughter: the Munster Fusiliers and Royal Dublin Fusiliers attempt to land from the converted collier River Clyde under direct fire from a Turkish position 200 yards inland. Of the first 200 men out of the ship, 21 reach the beach unhurt. The other beaches go better but inland fighting stalls within a mile.

phases.title: ANZAC Cove
phases.narration: The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps lands at the wrong beach, a kilometer north of the planned Gaba Tepe, in a small cove dominated by steep cliffs and the heights of Chunuk Bair and Sari Bair. The terrain is impossible for the planned advance. The ANZACs claw up the slopes but Mustafa Kemal, on his own initiative, orders his reserves to the heights with the famous instruction 'I do not order you to attack, I order you to die.' The ANZAC line stalls less than a kilometer inland.

phases.title: Stalemate
phases.narration: Both sides dig in. The shallow beachheads at Helles and ANZAC become trench networks in a few weeks. The Allies launch three battles for the village of Krithia on the Helles front. All three fail and produce 20,000 casualties. Disease (dysentery, enteric fever) becomes a heavier killer than Ottoman fire. The British add three more divisions and plan a third landing further north, at Suvla Bay.

phases.title: Lone Pine and The Nek
phases.narration: The August Offensive opens with a diversionary Australian attack at Lone Pine, taken at the cost of 2,000 Australian casualties and seven Victoria Crosses. The same morning the 8th and 10th Light Horse charge across 40 yards of open ground at The Nek, in three successive waves, into Ottoman trenches behind a curtain of fire. The artillery bombardment stops seven minutes early, giving the defenders time to remount their machine guns. 372 Australians become casualties in 45 minutes.

phases.title: Suvla Bay
phases.narration: The British IX Corps lands at Suvla Bay against weak Ottoman resistance. General Stopford has no plan beyond the landing and his men spend the next two days bathing in the sea while the heights inland sit empty. By the time Stopford orders an advance, Mustafa Kemal has personally ridden up Tekke Tepe with the Ottoman 8th Division at his back and seized the high ground at dawn on the 9th. The last best Allied opportunity to break the deadlock is thrown away.

phases.title: Withdrawal
phases.narration: London replaces General Hamilton with General Monro, who recommends evacuation. Lord Kitchener concurs. Across two nights at ANZAC and Suvla, and then over two weeks at Helles, the Allies pull 105,000 men, 5,000 horses, and 300 guns off the beaches without a single fatal casualty. The evacuation is the only Allied operation of the campaign that goes well. Allied losses for the eight-month campaign: about 56,000 dead, 124,000 wounded. Ottoman losses: about 87,000 dead, 165,000 wounded. Mustafa Kemal emerges as a national hero and a decade later founds the Republic of Turkey.

shiloh-1862.title: Shiloh: The Hornet's Nest
shiloh-1862.intro: April 1862. Grant's Army of the Tennessee camps at Pittsburg Landing on the Tennessee River, waiting for Buell's Army of the Ohio to march up from Nashville. Albert Sidney Johnston attacks first. Two days of fighting around a small Methodist meeting house, Shiloh, produce 23,746 American casualties, more than all previous American wars combined.
shiloh-1862.battlefieldDesc: Tennessee River bends east of Pittsburg Landing. Federal camps spread west across rolling farm country toward Shiloh Church and Owl Creek. Snake Creek separates the Federal right from the river.

phases.title: Surprise at Shiloh
phases.narration: Johnston's 40,000 march 22 miles in three rainy days from Corinth and form for attack within a mile of Sherman's pickets. At dawn the Confederate corps strike Sherman's and Prentiss's camps. Federal regiments break and run for the Landing. Others, Prentiss's, B. M. Prentiss in the center, pull back to a sunken farm lane and hold.

phases.title: The Hornet's Nest
phases.narration: Prentiss and W. H. L. Wallace hold a sunken farm road against eleven Confederate frontal assaults. The dense thicket and concentrated rifle fire give the position its name. Around 14:30 Johnston is hit in the leg by a stray ball, the femoral artery, and bleeds to death in minutes. Beauregard takes over and shifts to envelopment. Prentiss surrenders 2,200 men at sundown, having bought Grant the day.

annotations.text: Johnston dies of a wound he might have survived if a tourniquet had been applied. The Confederacy loses its most senior western commander.

phases.title: Buell arrives
phases.narration: In the rain after dark, Buell's lead division crosses the Tennessee on a captured ferry. Lew Wallace's Federal division finally arrives from upriver. Grant now has 25,000 fresh troops. Beauregard's army sleeps in Federal camps in the Shiloh fields. Grant, asked by Sherman whether to retreat: "Retreat? No. Lick 'em tomorrow."

phases.title: The counterattack
phases.narration: At dawn Grant attacks. Refreshed Federal divisions push the exhausted Confederates back across the same ground they took the day before. By midafternoon Beauregard, his line crumbling, orders withdrawal to Corinth. Grant, who lost 13,000 in two days, more than the country has ever lost, keeps the field, but the political cost almost ends his career. Lincoln defends him: "I can't spare this man. He fights."

annotations.text: 23,746 American casualties, more than all previous American wars combined. The country realizes the war will not be brief.

dien-bien-phu-1954.title: Dien Bien Phu: The End of an Empire
dien-bien-phu-1954.intro: March 1954. French paratroopers build a fortified airhead in the remote Dien Bien Phu valley near Laos, bait to draw the Viet Minh into a set-piece battle on French terms. Giap surprises everyone by dragging artillery up the surrounding mountains. After 56 days of siege, France's eight-year war in Indochina ends, and so does French Indochina.
dien-bien-phu-1954.battlefieldDesc: Saucer-shaped valley in northwest Vietnam. French strongpoints form a ring around the central airstrip. Named (per the legend) after Colonel de Castries's mistresses, Béatrice, Gabrielle, Anne-Marie, Dominique, Eliane, Claudine, Huguette, Isabelle to the south.

phases.title: The valley fortress
phases.narration: Operation Castor drops 16,000 French troops into the valley to interdict Viet Minh supply lines toward Laos. Colonel de Castries fortifies a ring of strongpoints around the airstrip. The French expect Giap to attack with infantry through low ground where airpower and artillery will destroy him. Giap has other plans: he has spent four months dragging 200 artillery pieces up the surrounding ridges by hand and pulley.

phases.title: Béatrice and Gabrielle fall
phases.narration: At 17:00 on 13 March a single Viet Minh shell decapitates the Foreign Legion battalion command on Béatrice. The strongpoint falls in six hours. Gabrielle falls the next night. The airstrip is now under direct fire and unusable in daylight. The French artillery commander, Colonel Piroth, can find no targets, Giap's guns are in pits and caves, and commits suicide with a grenade in his bunker.

annotations.text: Piroth: "I am completely dishonored." He pulls the pin lying on his cot.

phases.title: The five hills, and air supply
phases.narration: Giap launches a five-week assault on the central ring of strongpoints, Dominique, Eliane, Huguette, Claudine. Trenches creep forward at night, Vauban-style. Resupply is by parachute from C-47 Dakotas flying through anti-aircraft fire. Thousands of containers drift into Viet Minh lines. American C-119s flown by CIA-contracted pilots take heavy losses. French reinforcements parachute in until the perimeter shrinks too far to receive them.

phases.title: Surrender
phases.narration: On 7 May the last strongpoints, Eliane 2, Claudine 5, fall to direct assault. De Castries radios Hanoi: "The Viets are everywhere. The situation is very grave. Au revoir, mon général." His command bunker is overrun at 17:30. 10,000 French Union troops walk out as prisoners. Only 3,000 will survive the march to Viet Minh camps. The next morning the Geneva Conference opens.

annotations.text: The Geneva Accords partition Vietnam at the 17th parallel. The US position deepens, ten years later becoming the war we now call Vietnam.

pharsalus-48bc.title: Pharsalus: Caesar's Fourth Line
pharsalus-48bc.intro: 9 August 48 BC. Caesar's veteran army of 22,000 faces Pompey's 45,000, fed by the Republic's senatorial faction, on the plain of Pharsalus in Thessaly. Pompey plans to crush Caesar's right wing with cavalry. Caesar conceals a fourth line of infantry to receive that very charge.
pharsalus-48bc.battlefieldDesc: Plain near Pharsalus in Thessaly, between the Enipeus River to the south and rising ground to the north.

phases.title: Deployment
phases.narration: Pompey's right anchors on the Enipeus. He sets his strongest legions on his left, supported by 7,000 cavalry under Labienus. Caesar mirrors with his own anchor on the river but his left, opposite Labienus's cavalry, is dangerously thin. Behind his right Caesar quietly forms a fourth line, six cohorts pulled from each of his three legions there, held in reserve at a right angle to the main line.

phases.title: The cavalry charge
phases.narration: Pompey orders Labienus's cavalry forward to sweep Caesar's left, then loop behind the line and roll it up from the rear. The mass of horse breaks Caesar's token cavalry and turns the flank. Pompey's plan is working. Just then Caesar's hidden fourth line stands up, and Caesar has given them an unusual order: drive your pila at the cavalry's faces.

phases.title: Pila in the face
phases.narration: Caesar's veterans use their pila as thrusting spears, aimed at the riders' faces, knowing well-born young Roman cavalrymen will recoil from being scarred. Labienus's horse breaks. The fourth line keeps going and rolls up Pompey's exposed infantry left wing, while Caesar's main line, held back to be fresh, advances frontally across the plain.

phases.title: Flight
phases.narration: Pompey, watching his line collapse from the rear, rides off to his camp, takes off his general's cloak, and flees east. His army disintegrates. Caesar walks the field and famously says, looking at the senatorial dead: "They wanted it this way." Pompey reaches Egypt seeking refuge. He is murdered on the beach by Ptolemy's courtiers as he steps from the boat.

annotations.text: The end of the Roman Republic in fact, if not yet in name. Caesar rules alone from 48 BC to the Ides of March 44 BC.

sekigahara-1600.title: Sekigahara: The Defection at Noon
sekigahara-1600.intro: Twenty-first of October, 1600. Tokugawa Ieyasu marches the Eastern Army into a narrow pass in Mino province where Ishida Mitsunari's Western Army has held the heights since before dawn. Eighty thousand men on each side. Fog so thick on the floor of the pass that the lines cannot see each other at first light. The Western Army holds the better ground. The Eastern Army holds something more useful. A letter, signed weeks earlier, from one of the Western generals.
sekigahara-1600.battlefieldDesc: The Sekigahara pass on the Nakasendō highway. Wooded mountains close on the north, Mount Matsuo dominates the southern flank. The road runs east to west along the floor.

phases.title: Deployment in the Fog
phases.narration: Ishida posts his army across the northern heights and along the southern slope of Mount Matsuo. Kobayakawa Hideaki takes Matsuo with fifteen thousand men. Ōtani Yoshitsugu, sickly and carried in a litter, sits at the base of Matsuo with five thousand. The Eastern Army arrives in column and deploys along the floor of the pass before the fog has begun to lift.

units.label: Shimazu Yoshihiro on the Western left

phases.title: The Lines Close
phases.narration: The fog burns off. Ii Naomasa, who has been forbidden the honour of opening the battle, fires the first matchlock anyway. Eastern infantry advances up the floor of the pass. Ukita and the Western centre charge down to meet them. The action becomes general within the hour.

movements.label: Ii Naomasa fires the first shot

phases.title: Indecisive Hours
phases.narration: The lines grind against each other in the centre. Shimazu refuses to advance from the Western left. Mōri, posted in the far rear, never moves. A letter from Tokugawa has bought his neutrality. On Mount Matsuo, Kobayakawa watches and does nothing. Tokugawa, growing impatient, orders his arquebusiers to fire a volley up the slope. It is a signal, not an attack.

units.label: Mōri Hidemoto, neutralised in the rear

movements.label: Volley fired up Mount Matsuo to force the issue

phases.title: Kobayakawa Defects
phases.narration: Kobayakawa orders his fifteen thousand down the southern slope of Mount Matsuo. They do not attack the Eastern Army. They attack Ōtani. The man Kobayakawa had been ordered to support all morning watches the army he had been promised charge into his flank.

units.label: Ōtani, betrayed at the foot of Matsuo

phases.title: Collapse
phases.narration: Ōtani holds for an hour against the new attack from the side, then is overwhelmed. With his position taken, the Western centre is unhinged. Ishida's army dissolves westward through the Nakasendō pass. Shimazu cuts an immortal retreat straight through the Eastern lines and rides home. Ishida, captured days later, is executed in Kyoto. Tokugawa Ieyasu has won Japan.

movements.label: Western collapse westward down the pass
Shimazu rides through the Eastern lines

mariupol-2022.title: Mariupol: Eighty-Two Days
mariupol-2022.intro: Late February 2022. Russian and DPR columns converge on the port city from Donetsk to the east and Crimea to the west. The ring closes by the first of March. Eighty-two days later the last defenders walk out of an underground steel plant on the eastern edge of the city. By then the city is a ruin.
mariupol-2022.battlefieldDesc: Mariupol on the Sea of Azov. Port and rail yards on the southern shoreline, residential districts north of the centre, Azovstal steelworks at the south-east edge against the Kalmius river.

phases.title: The Ring Closes
phases.narration: Russian armour rolls west out of Donetsk while naval infantry pushes east from Berdyansk and Crimea. The two columns meet north of the city in the first days of March. Mariupol's land corridor to the rest of Ukraine is cut. The siege begins.

phases.title: Block by Block
phases.narration: Artillery and air strikes walk in from every cardinal direction. The Drama Theatre, marked DETI (children) on its roof, is bombed on the sixteenth of March with hundreds sheltering inside. The Mariupol Hospital is hit days earlier. Ukrainian Azov Regiment and 36th Marine Brigade trade fire down arterial roads in armoured fighting vehicles and on foot. The civilian death toll begins to be counted in the thousands.

movements.label: Northern axis presses into the centre

phases.title: Into Azovstal
phases.narration: The Ukrainian command consolidates inside the Azovstal steelworks at the south-east edge of the city. The plant is a sprawling Soviet-era complex of bunkers, galleries, and underground passages built deep enough that no surface-launched munition reaches the lowest levels. Civilians shelter in the same tunnels. Russian forces seal the perimeter and shift to bombardment.

phases.title: Underground
phases.narration: Russian air strikes target the plant for weeks. Bunker-buster munitions are reported. The defenders broadcast appeals from underground galleries with cracked ceilings and emergency lighting. Civilians are extracted under a UN- and ICRC-brokered corridor. The garrison continues to fight from the deepest levels.

phases.title: Surrender at Azovstal
phases.narration: Kyiv orders the garrison to stand down. Over a thousand defenders walk out of the plant under Russian guard. Many will be exchanged later. The Mariupol Drama Theatre, the maternity hospital, the apartment blocks of Prymorskyi district are all in the public record. The city has fallen. The defenders have entered the national memory.

units.label: Russia and DPR in the city

movements.label: Garrison exits Azovstal under Russian escort

hostomel-airport-2022.title: Hostomel: The Airport Drop
hostomel-airport-2022.intro: Twenty-four February 2022. A Russian air assault force lifts from Belarus before first light and sets course for Antonov Airport at Hostomel, twenty miles north-west of Kyiv. The plan is simple. Take the apron, hold it for an hour, fly in heavy reinforcements, drive on the capital that same day. The runway has other ideas.
hostomel-airport-2022.battlefieldDesc: Antonov Airport, Hostomel. The apron runs east-west, the woods of Hostomel close on the north and south, the M07 highway from Kyiv lies along the east edge.

phases.title: Helicopter Strike
phases.narration: Thirty-four helicopters cross the Dnipro at low altitude. Ka-52 gunships peel off to suppress the Ukrainian National Guard company holding the apron while Mi-8 transports settle onto the tarmac. Paratroopers spill out, fan along the runway, and take the eastern half of the field within the hour.

movements.label: Mi-8 air assault lands on apron

phases.title: Counter-Attack from the Woods
phases.narration: Ukrainian Air Assault Brigade elements race north from Kyiv on the M07 highway and dismount in the treeline east of the runway. Artillery batteries firing from positions further south register the apron. The paratroopers, dug in among the parked transport planes, find themselves pinned without the reinforcements the plan required.

movements.label: Air Assault Brigade onto the apron

phases.title: Cratering the Runway
phases.narration: Ukrainian artillery, fired from positions outside the airport, walks rounds across the tarmac. Concrete cracks, the runway lights die, the centre line opens into trenches. Whatever lifts from Pskov next will have nowhere to land.

phases.title: The Night Holds
phases.narration: Russian paratroopers consolidate at the eastern end of the field, where their helicopters still squat among the wrecked Mi-8s. Ukrainian forces hold the western half and the surrounding woods. No transport ever lands. The air bridge to Kyiv is closed before midnight.

phases.title: Withdrawal Toward Bucha
phases.narration: Russian airborne and ground forces, never reinforced as the plan required, fall back south-east along the Bucha and Irpin axis. Ukraine reoccupies the apron and finds what is left of the Mi-8 fleet on the tarmac. The airport that was supposed to open Kyiv ended up closing it.
